summary: Local differential privacy (LDP) has become a crucial paradigm for privacy-preserving graph analytics, enabling graph analytics tasks such as subgraph counting without requiring a trusted curator. However, while LDP provides strong privacy guarantees, the integrity and robustness of LDP subgraph counting protocols in the presence of malicious participants remain poorly understood. In particular, since data are randomized locally before collection, it is inherently difficult to distinguish malicious users from honest ones based solely on their submitted reports, and small, protocol-compliant local manipulations can be systematically amplified through reconstruction and calibration into large global estimation bias. In this paper, we use LDP triangle counting as a representative task to characterize the vulnerability of LDP subgraph counting to data poisoning attacks. For both non-interactive and interactive LDP triangle counting protocols, we analyze their attack surfaces and develop a unified gain-driven framework that captures how adversarial users can manipulate calibrated subgraph count estimates, which we instantiate on representative protocols of both types. Extensive experiments on four real-world graph datasets demonstrate that these attacks can significantly distort triangle count estimates across different protocols and adversarial settings. Moreover, we show that existing and straightforward defenses are insufficient to mitigate these attacks, underscoring the need for robustness mechanisms tailored to LDP subgraph counting.

title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
summary: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.
comment: 55 pages, 9 tables. Code, logs and data: [Zenodo DOI, add after upload]

title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
summary: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.

title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
summary: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.
comment: 22 pages. Presented at the KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI (ETAAI; non-archival). Code and trial ledgers: https://github.com/dowlingwong/autoresearch_harness (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24174991)

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
summary: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation at CoRL 2026

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs
summary: Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.

title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
summary: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

title: CratesBump: A Version-Bump Dataset for the Rust Ecosystem
summary: We release CratesBump, the first public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, together with semver-extract, the tool that builds it. CratesBump is built from every crate on crates$.$io with at least two releases before 14 September 2026 (about 220,000 crates), giving over two million consecutive release pairs. Each pair has 41 features (code changes from AST diffs, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence, GitHub commit and issue activity), its source repository where listed, and two labels: the literal reading of MAJOR$.$MINOR$.$PATCH, and Cargo's rule, under which a 0.y bump is a breaking change. semver-extract regenerates the dataset from public crates$.$io data and the GitHub API. To illustrate its use we (i) benchmark bump predictors on held-out repositories, finding the task learnable but far from solved, with lower scores on later releases; (ii) measure which feature groups carry the signal; (iii) check, against declared dependency ranges, how often Cargo's rule shields dependents from pre-1.0 breaking releases; and (iv) audit a sample of releases with cargo-semver-checks, finding minor and patch releases that break the public API despite their version number. Dataset and tool are released under open licenses.
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Dataset and tool: https://github.com/muhammad-hassnain/CratesBump

title: LightSEAD: Lightweight SE(3)-Aware Keypoint Detector through Selective Knowledge Distillation
summary: The pursuit of improved performance in deep learning has often been accompanied by increasing architectural complexity and computational demands. We explore an alternative direction: achieving more with less through structured supervision. We introduce LightSEAD, a lightweight SE(3)-aware keypoint detector initialised with calibrated Harris pseudo-labels and enriched through viewpoint-aware and appearance-aware supervision and selective knowledge distillation. LightSEAD comprises only six convolutional layers and 84,289 learnable parameters, achieving competitive repeatability across HPatches, KITTI 06 and 4Seasons while demonstrating its downstream applicability to relative pose estimation on MegaDepth-1500. Further optimised for mixed-precision inference, LightSEAD Coarse achieves approximately 909 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 and 139 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano Super.

title: Protecting Web Applications using a Multimodal AI-based System for Classifying Web Injection Attacks
summary: Web applications have been essential to accessing and managing online services. Made available with weaknesses, much due to their rapid development and human error, they are exposed to frequent web injection attacks, leaving security analysts overwhelmed with threats and alerts that often lack critical details for proper risk assessment. Detecting these attacks requires inspecting the payload of network traffic packets, which becomes inaccessible when traffic is encrypted via HTTPS, as encryption hides the content of the traffic. This paper introduces a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to protect online services that rely on web application security by detecting and classifying web injection attacks, and provides security analysts with information to support attack prevention and incident response. The system employs unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) to flag potentially anomalous Network Flows (NetFlows). The corresponding data recorded in Web Server Logs (WebLogs) is then analysed using a heuristic framework based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised ML to detect and classify web injection attacks. Finally, the resulting classifications are scrutinised using a Similarity Search Engine (SSE) based on Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to validate them. The solution handles encrypted traffic by analysing NetFlows and WebLogs, the latter in their natural, unencrypted form, by leveraging NetFlow-level metadata for anomaly detection and analysing web server logs after TLS termination, thereby avoiding any additional in-network traffic decryption. It was evaluated in the classification of eight web injection attack classes. The results demonstrated its ability to accurately identify attacks and their classes, achieving an F_1 score of 91% and an accuracy of 95%, and offering valuable insights for alert prioritisation.

title: Same Model, Different People: Numerical Execution Contracts and the Reproducibility of Fairness Audits
summary: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, but the arithmetic that evaluates it is part of that function. This study holds the model, records, threshold and audit code fixed and varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers. Tier 1 changes only how products and sums are computed, with the serialized weights byte-identical, and is the causal test of arithmetic. Tier 2 runs reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16 compute, FP8 and 8-bit weights), which can also round weights and change engines and kernels, so its effects belong to the configuration. It audits three tabular model families and two open-weight language models (4B and 24B parameters) on four public tasks, including hospital readmission, on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. Tier 1 changed decisions near the threshold, and which ones depended on the GPU and its software stack, but no verdict under the prespecified, unweighted tests. Tier 2 configurations changed more decisions and some diagnostic verdicts, but no four-fifths verdict. Serving the 24B model with vLLM FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its strict FP32 reference failed: its demographic-parity and equalized-odds gaps fell from 0.0567 and 0.0515 to 0.0417 and 0.0394, against a diagnostic tolerance of 0.05. At the reference's selection count FP8 failed demographic parity, and no reading gave its equalized-odds change a paired interval excluding zero. The declared audit depends on the configuration; FP8 is not shown to be fairer. At the frozen thresholds, every pass-fail verdict a configuration changed had a sampling interval containing its criterion. It proposes an audit stability protocol in which the auditor declares contracts, groups, weights and tests before scoring and records each verdict's range over them apart from its sampling uncertainty.

title: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative
summary: Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires information about both distance and relative motion. Range-based filters commonly reconstruct the required range rate from successive range measurements or from obstacle-state estimators, which can introduce estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler. We use this measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF) and obtain a closed-form filter on the robot's forward velocity. A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. In 508 paired encounters within the platform's retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter. On a Unitree Go1, the controller stops at $0.777 \pm 0.015$ m against the predicted $0.758$ m and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains. The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections. Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.

title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
summary: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
summary: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
summary: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. 27 pages

title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
summary: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models. A small steering actor selects a direction through a fixed low-rank random projection, while our norm-controlled construction keeps the resulting noise near the typical scale of a Gaussian sample. This separates the actor's control dimension from the full noise dimension, enabling steering of both video and action inputs. Across three world-action models and ten model-task pairs, video steering improves average success by 26.2 percentage points over the base policy, compared with 7.1 points for DSRL action steering. For smaller action policies, the same construction achieves comparable final success while generally improving early-training success. Steering actors trained in simulation also transfer to three physical bimanual manipulation tasks across two base policies, without additional real-world training.

title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
summary: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.

title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
summary: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
summary: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

title: VIBRA: Backward-Compatible Cross-Modal Retrieval with Consensus Barycenters
summary: Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query. We propose VIBRA, which matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects the errors of a single model with the barycenter of several views, which is itself a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, so that models absent at deployment still shape every query. We show that the barycenter gains margin over the average of its views exactly when their hardest irrelevant items differ, and we characterize the share of this gain that one encoder can reach. On five benchmarks with five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA is the best compatible method in all 50 settings, improving Recall@1 by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and by up to 18.0 points over the old model, while adding less than 1 ms to the latency of the new encoder.

title: A-Tag: Cryptographic File Tagging with Enforced Live Human Presence
summary: The increasing autonomy of software agents and the proliferation of AI-generated content have weakened the reliability of digital actions as evidence of human involvement. Existing mechanisms, such as digital signatures and authentication protocols, verify identity and integrity, but do not establish whether a live human was present at the time an action was performed. In this paper, we introduce A-Tag, a system for verifiable human-in-the-loop tagging of digital artifacts. A-Tag cryptographically binds a file to a verified instance of live human presence at the moment of tagging. The resulting tag serves as a persistent and transferable proof that the action was triggered by a live human, without making claims about the origin, identity of the actor, or semantic content of the file. A-Tag is a modular framework combining liveness verification based on micro-motion signals shaped by human motor control, a secure cryptographic binding between the verified event and the artifact, and a publicly verifiable logging mechanism enabling independent validation. We formalize security properties of human presence signals, define an adversarial model capturing automated and relay attacks, and analyze the system's guarantees and limitations. We implement A-Tag on commodity devices and evaluate it under realistic conditions. Our evaluation shows that A-Tag provides cryptographically sound artifact binding with deterministic verification, while enabling robust recovery under real-world transformations, achieving over 99 percent success for image-based artifacts, and maintaining sub-second verification and practical tagging latency.

title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
summary: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
summary: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
summary: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.

title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
summary: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

title: LuxTac: A Flexible, Scalable, and Open-Source Optical Taxel Array with Distributed Three-Axis Force Sensing for Tactile Robot Learning
summary: Low-cost tactile arrays have made touch a practical input for robot learning, but piezoresistive designs sense only pressure, while camera-based sensors that also resolve shear are too bulky to tile over a gripper. To solve this problem, we present LuxTac, a flexible, scalable optical taxel array, about 3.5 mm thick and built from off-the-shelf parts. Each taxel is a digital RGBC light-to-digital converter under a translucent white silicone layer capped by an opaque black film, so the back-scattered LED light falls monotonically with local indentation depth. The same board accepts two interchangeable gel cartridges: a plain one for normal sensing, and one with colored walls that encodes the local shear in the color of the returned light, with no camera, magnets, or bump overlay, making LuxTac, to our knowledge, the first optical taxel array to resolve shear at individual taxels. Characterized with an automated CNC indenter and a six-axis force/torque sensor, the normal cartridge responds linearly to force ($R^2$ = 0.999) from 104 mN to at least 5.8 N, with 2.0% repeatability, 5.9% hysteresis, and a taxel-to-taxel variation of 6-10% after normalization. With the shear cartridge, per-taxel models estimate the three-axis force at every taxel; across three indenter shapes and nine held-out sessions, the summed estimates reach $R^2$ = 0.96/0.96/0.92 in x/y/z, each taxel's estimate 0.92/0.93/0.94, and the median shear-direction error is 4.8 degrees. Adding LuxTac pressure readings to an Action Chunking Transformer policy substantially improves peg-in-hole success over a vision-only baseline. Design files, code, and videos are available at https://luxtac.github.io.
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Project page: https://luxtac.github.io

title: Apply All, Prove Once: Embedding Parameterized Lemmas in DRAT
summary: The deletion-resolution-asymmetric-tautology (DRAT) proof format is widely used to express unsatisfiability proofs of Boolean formulas. Our DRATL format extends DRAT with parameterized lemmas, allowing a single proof to succinctly capture the common case where multiple instances of a pattern occur in a formula, differing in the identities and phases of the variables. Proofs expressed in DRATL can be hierarchical, with the proof of one lemma containing instantiations of others. Our elaborator program expands a DRATL proof containing multiple, nested lemmas into a standard DRAT proof. Most significantly, the elaboration yields compact proofs, where a single sequencing of the proof steps for each lemma covers all of its instantiations. Several case studies demonstrate that lemmas can provide a powerful method to generate short proofs for challenging problems.

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
summary: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
summary: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

title: Learning the Dynamics of Deformable Linear Objects Through Coupled Oscillators for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
summary: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $Φ$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $Φ$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $Φ$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.

title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
summary: Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity. We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
summary: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

title: From Docket Minutes to Case Trajectories: Building Analysis-Ready Criminal Court Data
summary: Criminal court records are often fragmented, noisy, and siloed, making it challenging for both legal experts and community stakeholders to access and analyze court data to identify trends and provide public oversight. In this paper, we introduce a system for data ingestion, harmonization, and dashboard visualization designed for New Orleans criminal court proceedings data, aimed at both expert and lay audiences. Our system collects and harmonizes disparate data, generates case trajectories, and provides intuitive visualization techniques based on community feedback to analyze demographics, temporal trends, and specific case events. We demonstrate the system through an exploratory analysis of recent short-term trends and policy impacts within New Orleans, illustrating how it can support the investigation of anomalies, policy changes, and procedural irregularities. We also present feedback from a small formative study of community stakeholders who have helped co-design and use the system, suggesting that it may improve access to and interpretation of local court data.
comment: This paper has been accepted at IEEE Big Data 2026

title: Ties at the Top: A Point-in-Time Comparison of CVSS and EPSS at a Fixed Budget
summary: Organizations must decide which vulnerabilities warrant further analysis and protective action when the volume of published vulnerabilities exceeds their analytical capacity. We present a methodology for comparing vulnerability-prioritization strategies under an explicit resource constraint, represented by a fixed number of CVEs selected from a common eligible population. We apply this methodology to the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). For CVEs published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) from 17 March to 31 December 2025 and from 1 January to 31 March 2026 (Q1), we reconstruct each CVE's scores and status 30 days after NVD publication, using archived source data. Each cohort has one ranking per strategy at a 5% budget. Positives are CVEs added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within 180 days after their decision day. The catalog is maintained by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). EPSS captures 16 of 40 positives in 2025, versus 5 for CVSS; alternative selections among tied CVEs cannot raise CVSS capture above 9. In Q1, CVSS captures 4 of 11 and EPSS 3, but tie-breaking can reverse this ordering. The score alone leaves most of each CVSS list undecided: the tie-breaking rule allocates 1,678 of 1,919 CVSS places in 2025 and 589 of 758 in Q1 among CVEs tied at score 9.8. Most chosen CVSS scores come from non-NVD providers; disabling those scores reduces CVSS capture from 5 to 1 in 2025 and from 4 to 0 in Q1. A fixed-budget comparison should therefore report its decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.

title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.

title: RESCUE Jumper: A Centimeter-Scale Rolling and Jumping Robot for Search and Rescue
summary: Centimeter-scale robots are promising for urban search and rescue because they can enter confined spaces that are inaccessible or unsafe for humans. However, their small size limits obstacle traversal after deployment. This paper presents the RESCUE Jumper, a 125 g mobile robot with a 6.2 cm width and 6.2 cm diameter wheels that combines ground rolling with jumping to traverse steps and gaps that exceeds its rolling capability. The RESCUE Jumper uses its two actuators for both rolling mode and jumping by reversing the direction of wheel motion. Forward wheel motion enables rolling, while reverse wheel motion winds a spring steel tail to store elastic potential energy and release it for jumping. The RESCUE Jumper varies tail winding speed to control jump direction, transitioning from backward to forward jumps as winding speed increases from 0.75 rad/s to 8.73 rad/s. The launch angle of the jumps ranges from 45 degree to -11 degree with respect to the vertical axis, reaching a maximum height of 9.2 cm and a maximum lateral displacement of 11.2 cm. We model the winding speed-dependent jumping behavior in three phases: tail release to determine the contact point and robot orientation, tail straightening until liftoff, and ballistic flight to predict jump height and lateral displacement. Finally, qualitative tests highlight the robot's locomotion in cluttered, real-world environments. The model and experiments presented in this work can inform future designs of space-constrained jump mechanisms in centimeter-scale robots for search and rescue and inspection in unstructured environments.

title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.
comment: Published in EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 37 pages. Code and data: https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors. Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2026.emnlp-main.2372/

title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
summary: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
summary: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.

title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution
summary: Sparse attention reduces computation, but distributed execution may still transfer unnecessary data and incur substantial per-operation overhead. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce these costs, but replanning for dynamic masks must be cheaper than the execution time it saves. We present DexAttention, a distributed sparse attention system that co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution. Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance computational load and reduce communication. A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and computation operations, while a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks. This division keeps detailed synchronization out of planning while enabling overlap without repeated attention launches. The framework supports static and dynamic per-head masks across multiple attention compute kernels. On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, DexAttention achieves a $1.39\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. For dynamic video attention, it achieves $2.11$--$2.37\times$ speedups over Ring Attention including planning.

title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
summary: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
summary: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

title: Learning and Control in Physically Coupled Dynamical Systems
summary: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.

title: BiCAT: Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization
summary: Autoregressive vision-language-action (VLA) models predict discrete action tokens with the next-token objective of their vision-language backbone, so the action tokenizer defines the interface between the policy and the robot. In bimanual manipulation, the two arms share a repertoire of movements yet coordinate through complementary roles, and an action representation should capture both. However, most existing tokenizers encode both arms as a single concatenated action vector, in which motion patterns common to the two arms are not shared and cross-arm dependencies remain entangled within each token. The policy must therefore learn both aspects implicitly. We propose Bimanual Coordination Action Tokenization (BiCAT), which shares one motion representation across arms while conditioning each arm's tokens on its partner through symmetric cross-arm attention and a joint decoder. The policy then predicts all tokens of each arm in parallel, generating the left arm first and the right arm conditioned on it. Across ten RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and six real-world tasks on three embodiments, BiCAT achieves the highest success among the compared tokenizers. In simulation, it improves mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines, with the largest gains on tasks that require close coordination between the arms, while requiring only 40.5 ms per action chunk. These results suggest that the action tokenizer is a natural place to model bimanual coordination.

title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
summary: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

title: Formal Adequacy Index (based on Polish-language material)
summary: Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.

title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
summary: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges.
