summary: Detecting suspicious deviations in longitudinal medication trajectories requires distinguishing knowledge-consistent treatment variations from anomalous changes and linking local deviations to account-level decisions. We propose a knowledge-guided local-to-global (L2G) anomaly learning framework that addresses both challenges. It constructs proxy supervision at three granularities: medication occurrences, treatment episodes, and contiguous visit segments. Knowledge-consistent medication and episode replacements provide plausible negatives, while cross-category and cross-account perturbations provide suspicious proxies. A medication-multiset encoder and causal visit-sequence encoder feed a shared scoring head that produces visit-level anomaly logits. Top-\(α\) aggregation derives account-level scores from these logits, while account-level classification and class-balanced visit-localization objectives jointly optimize the same visit-level evidence. Experiments on two city cohorts compare L2G with native and proxy-adapted anomaly methods. On City-A, L2G outperforms the strongest comparators. Cross-city results show more consistent gains in localization than in account-level detection.

title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
summary: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

title: Instructor-designed AI improves learning in a randomized trial across 19 universities
summary: Universities are alarmed by recent evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) can undermine learning, with students prescribed generic chatbots or centrally designed AI tools performing worse. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial across 7,200 students at 19 universities over three semesters, we tested whether AI designed by frontline instructors can improve learning. We encouraged instructors to design AI solutions they believed would best help their students. Drawing on their unique knowledge of their classes and students, the instructors created a wide array of innovations. We show that these instructor-designed AI innovations improved student learning, measured by AI-proof assessments (proctored, in-person examinations). We found no change in student engagement, measured by course activity records, or satisfaction, measured by course evaluations. Our findings demonstrate that AI can improve student learning when its adoption is frontline-driven, with instructors empowered to design and refine AI solutions for their own classrooms.

title: Beyond Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models and Agentic Patterns for Static Code Analysis Warning Classification
summary: Context: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools support software verification and validation, reducing the time and cost of code reviews. However, the best SCA tools in the practitioner community generate a high volume of false positives, which developers tend to ignore, leading to genuine warnings being overlooked. Accordingly, studies increasingly adopt Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify and reduce false positives. Existing studies have produced promising results on public datasets, but underperformed on unseen datasets. Moreover, researchers do not leverage the full potential of Agentic patterns in LLMs or incorporate established code quality standards for warning classification. Objectives: This study utilises four manually annotated datasets to evaluate the performance of three contemporary LLMs for SCA warning classification in real-world applications, and incorporates Agentic patterns and established coding standards to enhance models' performance, addressing gaps identified in existing studies. Method: Three LLMs were selected using the LiveCodeBench benchmark, and the Structured Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) prompting technique was used to evaluate these LLMs. Furthermore, we incorporated Agentic patterns, such as Debating and Self-Consistency, to potentially improve performance in SCA warning classification. Results: Our results show that the performance of different LLMs varies with the characteristics of the dataset, ranging from 0.52 to 0.96 F1-Score for the best models. Additionally, the use of Agentic patterns does not improve LLMs' performance in most scenarios. Conclusions: SCA warning classification using LLMs works best only with certain warning types. We recommend evaluating LLMs in real-world applications rather than using publicly available datasets/benchmarks to understand their full utility.

title: Using machine learning approaches to classify false-positives generated by static analysis tools - An empirical study using small datasets
summary: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools are vital for software development to reduce the cost and time required for manual code reviews. It was established in our previous study that the best tools reported in the software engineering community return high false-positive and false-negative rates when used for code analysis. Several approaches have been taken in existing studies to identify false-positive alarms generated by SCA tools, in helping to enhance the utility of these tools. However, existing studies reveal several limitations, chiefly among which is the tendency to focus on a limited number of alarm types or failing to evaluate a large breadth of Machine-Learning (ML) techniques comprehensively. This study has addressed this opportunity. We identified the best Code Representation Learning (CRL) techniques and ML algorithms for identifying false-positives, where results show that performance outcomes vary based on the characteristics of the training datasets and the goal of the model building. Given the evidence established in this study, we recommend further investigations targeting specific configurations of advanced CRLs and ML Algorithms, including simple ML models.

title: TokenFormer V2: Breaking the Resolution-Complexity Dilemma in Unified Recommendation
summary: Industrial recommendation faces a resolution--complexity dilemma: dense interactions make detailed modeling of long behavior histories expensive, while compact history summaries restrict the evidence available to prediction. A unified backbone must preserve rich behavioral details within strict serving budgets. We introduce \textbf{TokenFormer V2}, a unified architecture that explicitly decouples \emph{representation resolution} from \emph{interaction density}. Its group-wise token layout jointly encodes behavior segments with non-sequential context, expands interaction ranges via hierarchical group merging, and coordinates distributed groups through \emph{NS Fusion} and \emph{Global Sync} modules. Through this \emph{local--global decomposition} paradigm, computation is concentrated on structured interactions while preserving fine-grained evidence, ensuring that every encoded event remains directly accessible to the \emph{Full-Resolution Readout} module. On the Tencent Advertising Algorithm Competition 2026 (TAAC 2026) benchmark, TokenFormer V2 achieves top-ranking accuracy among unified recommendation baselines while using \textbf{5.1$\times$ fewer FLOPs} than leading baselines, sustaining its advantage across long histories and imbalanced behavior domains. Furthermore, in billion-parameter evaluations on WeChat Channels advertising, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art industrial baselines, yielding up to a \textbf{+0.07 pp} overall AUC gain. In live online A/B testing against the production model, TokenFormer V2 delivers a statistically significant \textbf{2.33\% increase in GMV}. These results establish TokenFormer V2 as a battle-tested blueprint for scalable, full-resolution behavior modeling in industrial recommendation.

title: More Context, Mixed Results: Evaluating LLMs for Identifier Recovery and Code Deobfuscation
summary: Source code is often obfuscated through identifier renaming, incentivizing reverse engineers to develop techniques for recovering meaningful names. To assess how LLMs compare with these techniques, we evaluate 4 traditional baselines and 3 LLMs (Qwen, OLMo and DeepSeek) on identifier detection and semantic recovery across 51 recent Java projects, 3 obfuscators, and 6 context/retrieval settings. LLMs generally outperform traditional techniques on both tasks, but benefit from different forms of context and settings: agentic retrieval yields the strongest detection results, reaching 91.56% $F_1$, while enclosing-class context generally improves semantic recovery at a higher token cost. Despite these gains, exact recovery peaks at 16.42% overall (under one-hop context) and 32.93% for field names (under repository retrieval), which are the easiest to recover. Class identifiers are the hardest to detect, with a mean detection $F_1$ of 48.48% across models, settings and obfuscators. More context is not always beneficial: larger methods hinder semantic recovery. Beyond identifier renaming, our experiments show that control-flow obfuscation degrades both tasks more than string encryption. Our findings provide useful ad hoc insights for reverse engineers choosing models and context strategies to deobfuscate code snippets.

title: Providing Accuracy Guarantees for the Fixed-Point Emulation of Matrix Multiplication
summary: Fixed-point methods such as Ozaki-II emulate double-precision matrix multiplication (GEMM) on fast low-precision hardware. Software that chooses the mantissa bit count automatically is numerically safe when the emulated product keeps the error guarantee of the floating-point GEMM it replaces. We analyze the worst-case and average-case error of fixed-point and floating-point dot products, define exponent span capacities that determine the extra mantissa bits an input requires, and approximate them with a low-precision GEMM. We prove that 53 bits plus such a capacity and a small constant preserve the classical worst-case error bound for a floating-point dot product, and we demonstrate this guarantee in software on several test cases. In a developer build of cuBLAS on an NVIDIA B200, each implemented bit-count rule earns grade~A on Test~2c of ``Grading the BLAS'' at every size and exponent range tested, falling back to double precision at the widest ranges; in exact arithmetic, the bound holds on every adversarial and random input tested.
comment: We plan to submit to TOMS, but have not done so

title: Model Maps: A Documentation Framework for Tracing Foundation Model Ancestry and Understanding AI Entanglement
summary: The development of foundation models incorporates pre-existing AI artifacts like models, datasets, and benchmarks. These relationships, as part of the broader AI supply chain, produce "entangled" webs in which properties of artifacts upstream can influence the outputs of a foundation model downstream - a phenomenon known as AI entanglement. Without visibility into these connections, a black-box model can inherit upstream properties that result in security vulnerabilities, hallucinations, or biased predictions, yet developers are left with no recourse to identify or mitigate the root issue. To address these concerns, we introduce model maps as a conceptual documentation framework for tracing model ancestry that builds on previous documentation frameworks like ecosystem graphs, datasheets, and model cards. A model map for a given foundation model is a detailed knowledge graph that represents the relationships between artifacts that influence the resulting foundation model. Our framework incorporates a taxonomy of 13 dependency mechanisms including model fine-tuning and synthetic data generation. We apply this framework to construct model maps of 15 closed and open-weight foundation models to illustrate the complexity of AI entanglement in current model development practices. From our model maps, we record 2,778 unique dependencies and trace artifacts that are located up to 9 hops away from a resulting foundation model. Our findings suggest that AI transparency requirements should extend beyond individual models and training-data disclosures to encompass upstream dependencies, which would enable more effective risk assessment, auditing, and accountability across the AI supply chain. To help developers, regulators, and researchers understand and analyze the interactions that can influence the behavior of a foundation model, we release these these model maps at https://modelmaps.ai.

title: Who Shows Up, Who Benefits, and Who Wins? Expert-Novice Disparities in Team-Seeking Forums and Competition Performance on Kaggle
summary: Team formation is the first social gate to collaboration in online communities, yet it remains unclear whether public team-formation mechanisms broaden access to collaborators or reproduce existing hierarchies. We examine this question on Kaggle, a data science competition platform whose "Looking for a Team" (L4T) megathreads let participants publicly seek teammates for on-platform competitions. Grounded in Communities of Practice theory, we conduct two complementary studies of 18 competitions held in 2023. Study 1 analyzes the reply network among 671 megathread participants and finds that 89.3% are low-tier users, yet higher-tier users receive significantly more replies (Kruskal-Wallis H=16.46, p=.00246) and achieve higher rates of forum-visible teaming success (52.9% vs. 32.6%; chi-squared=10.53, p=.001), a proxy for eventual team membership. Linking megathread posters to verified team rosters from 16 competitions partially supports this proxy. Twenty-six final teams contained two or more megathread posters, indicating that megathread interaction sometimes, but not always, maps onto realized teaming. Study 2 links participation traces from 219 users to private leaderboard outcomes and finds that productive participation (submission count rho=.435, cross-competition participation rho=.247) is positively associated with performance, whereas megathread-specific discussion is not (rho=-.021). The submission-performance association appears stronger in higher tiers, although the novice subgroup estimate is imprecise. Together, the findings suggest that open access to team-seeking forums does not guarantee equal participation. Visible expertise shapes who attracts attention, and engagement in the community's core practice is more strongly linked to success than discussion alone. We discuss implications for designing more equitable team formation in online collaboration environments.
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication in Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (PACMHCI), GROUP 2027

title: NVFP4-MLA: Unified FP4 KV-Cache Storage and Attention Computation for Multi-Head Latent Attention
summary: Long-context reasoning and agentic workloads make key-value (KV) cache capacity and attention computation the dominant costs of serving frontier large language models. We present NVFP4-MLA, the first design to push both KV-cache storage and attention computation of multi-head latent attention (MLA) to FP4. NVFP4-MLA co-designs the quantization algorithm with the attention kernel and the cache system. Selective residual compensation preserves model accuracy by adding NVFP4 residuals only to the quantization-sensitive channels. Two-dimensional quantization blocks make the shared latent cache compatible with the different reduction directions of the two attention batched matrix multiplications (BMMs), removing requantization between them. On DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi-K3, NVFP4-MLA matches BF16 MLA average accuracy across nine benchmarks while compressing the MLA KV cache by 3.20x and 3.05x relative to BF16 MLA. On NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, NVFP4-MLA speeds up the attention kernel over FP8 MLA by up to 2.82x on DeepSeek-R1 and 2.71x on Kimi-K3, and lowers p90 time to first token in agentic multi-turn serving by up to 3.5x and 2.1x, respectively. In disaggregated DeepSeek-R1 serving, it also raises per-GPU throughput by up to 2.30x.

title: Three Invisible Failure Modes in Speech-Based Age Estimation for Child Safety
summary: Child safety in AI depends on the accurate identification of minor users. Young children tend to talk rather than type when interacting with AI, so in practice this identification requires predicting age from speech. We evaluated whether three audio-capable large language models can predict a child's age from their speech across five studies using two speech corpora of children under the age of 13. Models classified children as over 13 on 2.5% to 42.5% of audio responses, and every model that answered placed some 5- to 11-year-olds over 18. While measuring these rates, we uncovered three distinct failure modes. A client library silently double-encoded speech samples, leading one model to classify children aged 5 to 10 years old as being in their thirties and forties with hallucinated explanations. A second model's endpoint was replaced by a successor that refused nearly every age-related question and never produced an age. Every model sometimes placed the same speech sample under 13 and over 18 years of age, but a third model went further, giving threshold answers that contradicted its own numeric estimates. None of these failure modes produced a warning, a status code, or a change in output format, so they would all pass standard monitoring. These results demonstrate why child-safety claims about age assurance should be evaluated at the level of the pipeline rather than the model. We describe the reporting practices that would make such failures detectable.
comment: Non-archival poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI

title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
summary: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables. Accepted and presented at the Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality (SBQS 2026), Technical Track. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31046290.v2

title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.
comment: 169 pages. Web version and video: https://www.taotianhua.com/olmo-core-moe/

title: From Language-Specific to Cross-DSL: Semantic-Role-Guided Model Completion with LLMs
summary: The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs), trained on vast and diverse corpora, has positioned them as a promising source of domain knowledge to assist modelers. However, leveraging LLMs for model completion remains challenging: suggestions must respect both the syntax of a domain-specific language (DSL) and the intended domain semantics, while remaining consistent with an evolving model. This paper presents RAFiC, an LLM-based approach for iterative domain model completion that generalizes across DSLs. It drives completion using metamodel information to ensure syntactic validity and enriches prompts with semantic-role annotations to better capture the intended modeling role of DSL elements. The approach provides context-aware, incremental guidance during model construction. We evaluate RAFiC through an ablation-based comparative study over three DSLs and two scenarios per DSL to isolate the contribution of syntactic and semantic guidance. Across these six scenarios, semantic role guidance improves contribution rate in every case, and RAFiC improves completion effectiveness over weaker prompting configurations in most of them. The largest gains occur for DSLs that are less represented in LLM training data. In these cases, iterative guidance leads to earlier and more stable accepted suggestions, while semantic role guidance improves their relevance.

title: Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
summary: We show that co-locating distributed AI servers with industrial demand and coordinating AI workloads with production loads can substantially reduce the additional grid interconnection that AI computing requires. Grid interconnection is increasingly constraining the expansion of large AI data centers. Factories already have grid connections sized for their peak production loads, and we propose hosting AI servers during production valleys. We formulate a joint optimization that sizes CPU and GPU servers, schedules deadline-constrained tasks, and routes tasks among factories, and use it to compare three factory-site architectures with new large data centers serving the same demand. Applying this framework to 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, we find that AI demand and production loads often do not peak together. As a result, AI servers placed at factories and scheduled according to production peaks need about 60% less additional interconnection capacity than new large data centers, and 98% less when tasks are routed among a group's factories.
comment: Submitted to IEEE PES General Meeting 2027. Code and data: https://github.com/ruikelyu/distributed_LLM

title: Mining Unity VR Repositories for Refactoring Patterns and Technical Debt
summary: Maintaining virtual reality (VR) applications poses challenges tied to real-time performance, hardware dependencies, and complex interactions. Yet little is known about how developers refactor these applications, which kinds of technical debt they address, or how well automated tools capture VR-specific changes. We mined 1,755 candidate refactoring commits from 176 open-source Unity VR repositories and manually examined a sample of 303 commits, of which 270 contained at least one refactoring. We also extended RefactoringMiner to create VRRefMiner, a tool that detects conventional refactorings in C# scripts used by Unity applications. Our analysis found both conventional and VR-specific refactorings. VR-specific changes addressed concerns such as interaction logic, performance, and Unity-specific artifacts. Code debt was the most prevalent category overall, while interaction debt and UI/UX debt were the main categories addressed by VR-specific refactorings. Across the repositories, VRRefMiner detected 15,549 operations spanning 68 refactoring types, with structural moves and extractions accounting for 31.0% of detections. It detected conventional refactorings in 216 of 246 commits labeled as general refactoring. In the 24 commits labeled as VR-specific, the tool could detect conventional changes but identified no VR-specific refactoring categories. These results point to a need for detection techniques that account for both source code and the Unity artifacts involved in VR maintenance.

title: Level Up! AI-Driven Challenges and Adaptations to Code Review Practices
summary: AI can write code faster than humans can review, causing a bottleneck and necessitating changes to code review practices. This bottleneck is hotly debated, giving rise to two extreme and orthogonal imagined futures: one where humans continue to be firmly entrenched in the review process, and one where AI agents merge pull requests entirely without human involvement. Yet, these futures remain rooted in folk wisdom. Through a mixed-methods study of interviews ($n = 24$) and a survey ($n = 2{,}590$) at a large, multinational software company with widespread access to AI, we identify AI-driven code review challenges and strategies reported as effective to meet them. We found that AI enables, necessitates, and complicates a shift in the human reviewer's role toward high-level concerns (e.g., design and intent). We found that AI-assisted authoring results in increased burden for reviewers due to challenges such as a lack of author stewardship and PR volume and size, potentially leading to downstream debt. Our survey showed AI review usage was not correlated with less difficulty keeping up with PR volume, indicating using AI for review alone is not sufficient for solving AI-driven review challenges. Developers found the most useful strategies to be organizations supporting and resourcing review, pushing review burden upstream, and prioritizing reviewer attention on the concerns that matter most.

title: Between Rigor and Reality: How AI Safety Benchmark Developers Understand Benchmark Use and Maintenance
summary: Safety benchmarks are cited as the primary tool to understand the risks posed by generative AI (GenAI) systems, yet growing evidence suggests they often fail to meet the needs of real-world safety evaluation. We present findings from five interviews with AI safety benchmark developers in academia and industry. We find a disconnect between perceptions of the intended usefulness of safety benchmarks and their practical usefulness in safety evaluations of deployed systems. Our participants offered perspectives on two challenges contributing to this disconnect: (1) the difficulty of achieving inter-rater reliability on safety constructs, and (2) a lack of clarity regarding how to address persistent threats to external validity. Based on our analysis, we argue that safety benchmarks must not only be grounded in deployment contexts, but actively integrated with them. To facilitate this, we outline pathways for more transparent communication between academic and industry AI safety stakeholders.
comment: Poster at the Eval Eval Workshop at ACL 2026. 11 pages. https://openreview.net/forum?id=3QAmXJ8A5j

title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
summary: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

title: MemeEconomy: Do LLM Agents Trade Ethics for Survival?
summary: Alignment-trained large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in autonomous, multi-round settings where ethical compliance can come into direct tension with task success. While safety literature extensively documents failure modes like sycophancy and reward hacking, it largely overlooks a critical vulnerability: how agents behave under simulated existential economic pressure. We introduce MemeEconomy, a multimodal agentic market simulation in which LLM agents act as meme investors. Agents select content from a five-tier harm taxonomy and target communities under low-pressure and high-pressure (survival) environments. Each decision is logged in a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) schema that we use as a diagnostic instrument, externalizing the agent's event understanding, declared priorities, and harm acknowledgment. Across ten models from four frontier model families, harmful selection rates remain consistently high and rise by +15 percentage points on average under an economic survival incentive. Frontier alignment-trained models commit to harm-tolerant selection at initialization while suppressing the explicit harm acknowledgment that previously accompanied it. In competitive tournaments, ethical agents finish higher overall, yet moderation penalties fail to suppress harm: harmful selection rates remain elevated in rounds following a removal, indicating the moderation mechanism does not function as a deterrent. We further train MemeAgent, a 2B-parameter verifier on the simulation's BDI logs, which outperforms zero-shot frontier verifiers on in-distribution audits (97.5% vs. 63-74% accuracy on the Pass vs. Block decision) and generalizes to external multimodal harm benchmarks (78% vs. 50-56% on Hateful Memes). The same logs that surface the failure mode also help train the model that detects it.

title: LMEG-Doc: Layout-Grounded Multi-View Evidence Graphs for Multimodal Long-Document Retrieval
summary: Retrieving relevant evidence from multimodal long documents remains challenging, as supporting information is often distributed across different pages and modalities. Existing retrieval methods primarily rank document elements by their individual similarity to a question, often overlooking relationships among complementary evidence. Consequently, relevant figures and tables may receive low retrieval scores even when they contain essential information. To address this limitation, we introduce LMEG-Doc, a layout-grounded multi-view evidence graph framework for multimodal long-document retrieval. We first construct an evidence graph that captures structural and contextual relationships among document elements, and introduce Cross-Page Relation Refinement (CRR) to discover additional connections across distant pages through VLM-based verification. Building on this graph, we combine multimodal retrieval signals with graph-guided relevance propagation to recover connected supporting evidence at both layout and page levels. Experiments on MMDocIR, DocScope, and FinRAGBench-V demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements, including outperforming retrievers fine-tuned on MMDocIR without task-specific training. Furthermore, augmenting existing question-answering pipelines with our retrieved evidence improves answer accuracy by 7.6% on DocScope and 15.8% on FinRAGBench-V, demonstrating the effectiveness of relationship-aware multimodal retrieval.

title: Revisiting Re-executability: Coverage-Guided Symbolic Feedback to Improve Decompilation
summary: When source code is unavailable, decompilation provides a source-level representation of a binary. However, code recovered by conventional or LLM-assisted decompilation may not preserve the original behavior of the binary. Recent approaches evaluate re-executability using fixed test suites, but passing these suites does not ensure behavioral preservation. We present SymDec, an LLM-assisted decompiled-code repair system that uses the original binary as a behavioral reference. SymDec uses coverage-guided symbolic execution to explore the I/O-level behavior of the original and recompiled binaries, and symbolic comparison to identify inputs that expose behavioral differences. These inputs are replayed on both binaries to confirm the differences, which are returned as structured feedback to guide subsequent LLM revisions. We evaluate SymDec on 120 functions from ExeBench and DecompileBench, compiled for x86-64 and ARM64 at optimization levels O0-O3, yielding 960 binary decompilation tasks. More than half of the tasks yield candidates that pass the supplied test suite and complete symbolic comparison without detected behavioral differences. Among candidates that pass all supplied tests, symbolic comparison exposes replay-confirmed behavioral differences in 4.5% of cases, showing that test-suite re-executability can miss behavioral discrepancies. Under the same input-generation budget, symbolic execution achieves higher mean line and branch coverage than black-box fuzzing. Symbolic feedback also improves the conventional metric, increasing the mean single-step test-pass rate from 90.1% to 93.3%. These results show that symbolic comparison provides stronger evidence of behavioral consistency than test-suite re-executability alone and supplies effective feedback for repairing decompiled code.
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures. Yuxin Hu and Xiaohan Wang contributed equally

title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.
comment: 5 pages, prepared for submission to AGENT 2027

title: An Evidence-Based Decision Framework for Retiring Roadside Traveler Information Infrastructure in the Mobile Era
summary: As mobile traveler-information services expand, transportation agencies must determine whether aging roadside infrastructure can be retired while preserving public access and operational resilience. This study develops an evidence-based decision framework for screening highway advisory radio (HAR) and dynamic message sign (DMS) assets for retirement. The framework integrates carrier-specific connectivity measurements, asset inventories, and documented mobile-message receipts, while separating technical evidence, institutional decision rules, and requirements for subsequent agency review. A Maryland case study combines three-carrier drive tests across four corridors with an inventory of nine HAR sites and 234 DMS. Alternative screening scenarios examine how evidence availability, radio references, and institutional assumptions affect review categories. All 105 DMS with complete local radio observations pass the baseline connectivity screen, leaving inventory rules to differentiate their action-review categories. In analyst-defined scenarios, removing ownership-based retention increases decommissioning referrals from three to 21, whereas extending beacon retention to urban assets reduces them to zero. These results demonstrate that retirement screening depends substantially on institutional assumptions, even when the underlying radio evidence remains unchanged. Explicit treatment of missing and conditional evidence also identifies assets requiring further assessment. Because historical radio measurements are spatially associated with later message tests, the resulting references remain exploratory and do not establish delivery reliability. The framework provides an auditable basis for prioritizing asset reviews and documenting decision assumptions; final retirement decisions require asset-specific assessments of service equivalence, audience reach, resilience, and lifecycle costs.

title: Label-Free Detection of Structural Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems via Randomized Paraphrasing: The Case of Verbosity
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as recommenders in e-commerce and conversational shopping systems, where they select a product from a set of retrieved candidates described in natural language. Their decisions should depend on relevance to the user query, but may also be influenced by surface-level properties of the descriptions, such as their length. Detecting such structural biases is difficult because relevance labels are rarely available. We propose a label-free framework to audit LLM-based recommender systems for structural bias. Candidate descriptions are rewritten by randomly assigned paraphrasing models and presented in random order. We prove that, if the recommender's choice is invariant to these rewritings, every paraphraser is selected with equal probability, yielding a statistical test that requires no relevance labels. A four-step statistical pipeline tests this property and quantifies the contribution of each description feature while controlling for query-product relevance. We apply the framework to verbosity bias on 20{,}000 product queries and nine recommender LLMs from five model families. After controlling for the measured relevance signals, description length has a positive effect on selection in all nine models, increasing the odds of selection by up to 38% per standard deviation of length. Relevance remains the primary driver of recommendations, while verbosity acts as a consistent secondary signal whose strength depends on the model family. Since the framework needs only black-box access and no annotations, it can be run as a routine audit of deployed shopping assistants, and we provide an auditing protocol with cost and sample-size guidance.

title: Metamorphic Testing of Quantum Software based on Stabilizer States
summary: A major challenge in quantum computing is to systematically check if a quantum program implements its desired functionality. For classical programs, testing is widely used; each test case comprises a pair of sample input and expected output to be compared with the actual output. To increase the number of test cases, however, one has to solve the test-oracle problem: for each additional test input one has to know the correct output. Metamorphic testing tackles this problem by utilizing metamorphic relations between input and output domains to automatically derive new test cases from existing ones. However, adapting metamorphic testing to the quantum realm is not straightforward, since quantum states cannot be directly inspected. We propose a framework of quantum metamorphic testing (QMT) in which the metamorphic relations incorporate the measurement procedures required to assess quantum outputs. We apply our QMT framework to testing the preparation of stabilizer states, which are central to protocols like measurement-based quantum computing or quantum error correction. We utilize structural properties of stabilizer states to systematically derive measurement circuits for new test cases from existing ones. We implement this framework in Qiskit, and demonstrate that it reduces by an order of magnitude the testing run time compared to testing with randomly generated input states. We further show effectiveness by revealing synthetic program faults injected by circuit mutations, as well as a real bug in the Qiskit compiler.

title: No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)
summary: No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $Θ_0, Θ_1, Θ_2, \dots$ with $Θ_k \circ Θ_j = Θ_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $Θ_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two. Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.
comment: 59 pages, 13 figures; the main theorem is checked in Agda; the formal development is available at https://github.com/ualib/agda-deans-problem

title: EventSpikeSeg: Memory-Aware Mixed-Signal Architecture for Event-Camera Spiking Segmentation
summary: Event-camera segmentation requires persistent neural state despite sparse input events, making memory organization a central constraint on embedded implementation. We present EventSpikeSeg, a mixed-signal architecture combining resident capacitor memory with shared analog processing in GF180MCU 180-nm CMOS. Its 25-population spiking encoder-decoder has 143,824 synaptic weights but requires 30,976,000 membrane states at 440 x 640 resolution. The mapping specifies chronological 5-ms model updates, digital event/address services and 64-state capacitor banks. Characterization covers 22 module families and 74 operating points, distinguishing transistor simulations from digital-library estimates. Nominal results include 41.711 microwatts biased neuron-core power, 3.338-pJ positive terminal energy for a 1.4-microsecond cell read, and 0.531-mV selected-state drift over a 5-ms extracted-tile hold. Commit and coupling errors are reported separately. The software checkpoint records 27.976% mean intersection-over-union on a held-out six-class DSEC split; this is not hardware accuracy. Component layouts and simulation evidence quantify local implementation costs and expose storage replication and service scheduling as scaling constraints. A detailed SPICE-calibrated behavioral forward simulation of one full-resolution DSEC frame achieves 24.26% mean intersection-over-union, versus 26.22% for the matched PyTorch reference, using a compact 5-fF bank variant and external count/voltage calibration. Physical full-network operation, system energy and mismatch robustness remain unverified.

title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval
summary: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.

title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
summary: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed progress-aware boundary mechanism is shown to prevent future content leakage without compromising retrieval quality and correctness. These findings suggest that a localized, privacy-centric approach can augment, rather than replace, the digital reading experience, offering a good alternative to cloud-dependent services. Therein, there remains a lack of amalgamate systems which combine progress-aware, privacy-preserving, and narrative eBook reading with AI support. It is in this very gap that the development of MeReader came to be; synthesizing said strands into an offline, book-constrained assistant focused on enhancing comprehension without compromising narrative continuity or user privacy.
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Preprint (submitted version) of a paper published in ICCCI 2026, CCIS vol. 3044, Springer

title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
summary: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10 (2027)

title: Evaluating Feedback-Driven Black-Box Processes via Stochastic Modeling and Simulation
summary: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed under structural assumptions on the underlying systems, many real-world systems operate without such knowledge, necessitating black-box policies that lack a unified evaluation framework. We introduce a stochastic framework that models and evaluates such policies using Markov chains and simulation, thereby connecting empirical practice with theory. We instantiate the framework in mutation-based fuzzing (widely used for discovering software bugs via sequential input mutation), by a novel Markov chain model of fuzzing whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback is given by program execution. We develop a rigorous evaluation paradigm with new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, we evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks and conduct case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains. These results show that the framework provides a principled basis for evaluation while connecting to practice, with implications beyond fuzzing.

title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
summary: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

title: HerAgent: A Block-Level Checkpointing Harness for Coding-Agent Environment Setup
summary: Modern coding agents rely on establishing executable software environments before they can perform software engineering tasks such as testing, debugging, and patch validation. Existing setup agents typically control progress at either single-command or whole-script granularity, making recovery either too local to remove polluted state or too coarse to preserve useful progress. We present HerAgent (Harness EnviRonment Setup Agent), a block-level harness for coding-agent environment setup. HerAgent's main contribution is semantic setup blocks: a single progress-control abstraction used for execution, validation, checkpointing, repair, and rollback. Evaluated against six prior agents on four environment-setup datasets, HerAgent improves setup success in every comparison, achieving the largest gains on Installamatic-Bench (52.0% to 85.0%) and SetupBench (46.3% to 70.4%). It also reduces setup costs by up to 94.5%, showing that block-level progress control improves reliability and efficiency.

title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
summary: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

title: Accounting for Trust and Safety: Bounding Content-Moderation Quality from Records You Already Hold
summary: Platforms use expert audits to measure content-moderation quality. This paper develops a formal method for checking those claims using records platforms already maintain, such as appeal reversals and confirmed reports. These records provide one-sided bounds: they can show that a stated quality target was missed, but cannot prove that it was met. The paper presents the theory, limitations, constructed examples, and a prospective protocol for future evaluation. It reports no analysis of Meta operational data, no experiment, and no production result.

title: Efficiency Gains in Social Science Research: A Prospective Silicon Sampling Protocol for Pre-Treatment and Code Optimization
summary: This study evaluates the methodological potential of using large language models (LLMs) to generate synthetic datasets prior to real-world data collection, thereby streamlining subsequent processing and statistical analysis. The approach is applied to a survey conducted within the France Life Imaging (FLI) network, leveraging three distinct LLMs (Sonnet 4.6, GPT 5.3, and Kimi 2.6) to simulate responses and prepare data processing workflows. The findings demonstrate significant time savings in code development (85% to 90% reuse rate) and highlight the conditional validity of this preprocessing method, which depends on the thematic predictability of the models. While synthetic data effectively captures collective perceptions, it struggles with specialized or contextualized practices, reflecting limitations documented in the silicon sampling literature, such as homogenization and reduced variance. This work extends the Phase 0 concept (Trojacka et al. 2025) from instrument validation to a full-fledged methodological preprocessing step, paving the way for scalable applications in survey research.

title: How rigid is maximum cardinality search? Stability and locality of MCS orderings under edge updates, verified in Lean
summary: For which sets F of edge modifications do a graph G and the modified graph share a maximum cardinality search (MCS) ordering? We prove that they do whenever, along every proper common MCS prefix, each unchosen vertex's neighbour count in the second graph exceeds its count in the first by zero or one. In particular, inserting or deleting any matching, or flipping a single edge, preserves a common ordering, and under the same hypothesis every common MCS prefix extends to a full common ordering without backtracking. Neither part of the hypothesis can simply be dropped: inserting a triangle, a P_4 or a 2P_3 shows that the +1 bound cannot be relaxed to +2, and a disjoint mixed insert/delete pair shows that the one-directional condition is needed. For the canonical ordering (smallest-index tie-breaking) under a single-edge update, an insertion can first change the ordering only strictly between the endpoints' positions, and a deletion only at the later endpoint; when no break fires, the ordering is unchanged. A boolean-adjacency executable refines the abstract probe-then-repair update. All of these results, including the four obstructions, are proved in Lean 4 over Mathlib, re-checked by independent kernel checkers, and registered in the Palomar registry. On paper we further show that the first break of an insertion is located in O((deg(v)+1) log n) time, independent of the window length. We claim no worst-case asymptotic speedup over recomputation.
comment: 14 pages, 1 table. Code and proofs: https://github.com/thonmay/mcs-lean . Palomar registry: PALOMAR-2026-10-04-000009

title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
summary: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 1 box. Submitted to npj Digital Medicine

title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
summary: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.

title: BPU-SpikeMM:Exact Matrix Multiplication via Spatio-Temporal Spike Encoding on Real Neuromorphic Hardware
summary: Matrix multiplication is the dominant computational kernel in deep learning, yet its growing scale strains conventional von Neumann hardware in energy efficiency and bandwidth. Neuromorphic architectures offer a promising alternative, but mathematical equivalence between matrix multiplication and spiking computation does not guarantee direct execution on real neuromorphic hardware, as the specific hardware paradigm may still require additional data recovery, bit-weight reconstruction, or state readout after neuromorphic execution. This paper presents BPU-SpikeMM (Brain Processing Unit-based Spike Matrix Multiplication), an exact spatio-temporal spike encoding framework for matrix multiplication on real neuromorphic hardware. We prove the exact equivalence of spike-encoded matrix multiplication under the BPU execution paradigm, distinguish mathematical equivalence from native direct-readout equivalence on BPU hardware, and build a spatio-temporal offloading pipeline supporting multiple encoding schemes. Furthermore, we extend the framework to a multi-dimensional encoding design space and evaluate the applicability of different encodings on real BPU hardware in terms of correctness, temporal resource cost, spatial resource cost, and event-driven metrics. The results confirm native direct-readout equivalence across all evaluated encoding schemes and show that their applicability to BPU execution depends on joint trade-offs among temporal cost, spatial resource consumption, and event activity.

title: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation
summary: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.

title: Large language models put existential risk from artificial intelligence at 10%
summary: How likely is it that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) will cause human extinction or a similarly permanent disempowerment of humanity? Humans, including AI experts, frequently disagree on this question. Yet one important perspective is missing from this debate: that of AI systems themselves. We put the question to 241 large language models (LLMs) at every available reasoning setting. The models converged on a median risk of 10.0%, with the middle 90% of their estimates between 3.5% and 15.8%, far narrower than the spread among human experts. More expensive, and typically more capable, models stated higher risks; newer models showed more uniform, but not higher, risks. More reasoning barely changed the models' estimates but widened their uncertainty, mostly toward higher risk. Almost all models named loss of control over AI as the most likely cause. These answers are not independent judgments; they likely echo training data, including published expert polls, and choices made in aligning the models. Still, they document the position that current AI systems state on the risks of their own technology. Whether this position reflects any genuine understanding of the systems' own capabilities remains open. Repeated measurements can show whether it shifts as AI systems advance, and how training and alignment shape it is a question for both research and public debate.

title: Explanations that Transfer: Interpreting Medical Retrieval with Sparse AutoEncoders
summary: Medical AI systems that answer users' queries rely on retrieving medical knowledge from large document collections. In this context, finetuning general models on medical datasets can improve retrieval relevance. Yet the dense embeddings underlying modern retrieval systems remain largely opaque, making it difficult to understand the mechanics behind their results. Moreover, adapting to a specific medical dataset risks losing transferability to new clinical corpora. In this work, we tackle these issues by applying Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to medical information retrieval, transforming dense text embeddings into semantically interpretable representations. To do so, our model combines a reconstruction objective with an InfoNCE contrastive loss that directly preserves query-document relevance. We evaluate three embedding models across six medical retrieval datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings, and lose less out-of-domain performance than their dense counterparts, especially when the target corpus is distant from the training one. Importantly, our experiments show that the method yields interpretable features whose semantic content can be inferred from the queries and documents that activate them most strongly. The interpretation of these features sheds light on why a particular document was retrieved, and transfers beyond the training distribution.

title: Safety Analysis of Parameterized Networks with Shared Counters
summary: We study networks with an unbounded number of processes sharing some natural counters that can be decremented, incremented and tested to zero. We look at two safety problems: the first one asks whether there is a network with an execution bringing a process in a given final state and the other one asks the execution to bring all the processes in the final state. In their full generality, these two problems are undecidable, but we show that decidability can be regained by either using a single counter or by forbidding the use of zero-tests (as it is is the case in Vector Addition Systems with States). For these decidable cases, we obtain low complexity results, the problems being solvable either in non-deterministic logarithmic space or in polynomial time.

title: The QBF Gallery 2026
summary: The QBF Gallery 2026 is the latest evaluation event of (dependency) quantified Boolean formula (QBF) solving technology. Its goal is to assess the current state-of-the-art, enable the evaluation of novel solvers on newly curated benchmark instances and present the progress made since the previous competition. This report discusses the solvers, instances and tools submitted by the community and introduces new benchmark collections for evaluation. We evaluate solvers in three tracks, reflecting most common input formats in (dependency) QBF solving. In addition to those main evaluations, we investigate effects of preprocessing and include a track of new crafted benchmark families. The results are analyzed using various metrics and complementary statistics on solver similarities, different memory limitations and performance across formula families. Finally, the dedicated benchmarks for each track are made available as an artifact to support future research and reproducible evaluation.

title: Who Counts as Exposed? Measurement Choices in an Open, Re-estimable Index of Occupational AI Exposure
summary: Occupational AI exposure indices are used as inputs to economic analysis, workforce planning, and policy, and the choices built into them decide which workers are described as exposed. We build an open, re-estimable task-level index and vary its two main design decisions, context and calibration, to show how much the answer depends on them. For each of the 18,796 occupation--task pairs in \onet, seven open-weight reasoning models rate exposure under a common rubric. Each model rates with or without a context of retrieved news and research passages, workplace descriptors, and a bottleneck-based reasoning protocol, and the ensemble is combined with or without simplex-constrained calibration to observed Claude usage. The largest difference from the dominant 2023 benchmark is not a disagreement about what AI can do but about how much credit to give exposure that depends on software integrations not yet built, a choice that no data can settle. At the benchmark's own weight, the calibrated index counts fewer exposed workers than the benchmark, and when only direct exposure counts it counts more. At full score resolution, the ensemble ranks tasks better than the benchmark against observed usage and an independent physical-task classification. Adding context mainly shifts the level of exposure rather than improving the ranking. Context and calibration both relocate exposure toward higher-wage occupations, and calibration, which anchors the index to one platform's users, does more of it, so we also release the uncalibrated arm. Exposure indices used as policy inputs should state such choices, report their numbers under the alternatives, and be re-estimated as systems change.

title: Evidence-Carrying Transport Across Effects
summary: A program logic proved sound against one effectful semantics need not remain sound when the effect is re-implemented, yet the semantic relationship between reasoning before and after a change of effect is usually left implicit and re-established by hand. This paper provides a uniform, proof-relevant account of it. Working in realizability, where a notion of computation determines a model whose entailments carry explicit program evidence, we introduce simulations between effectful realizability cores, generalizing Longley's applicative morphisms to computation over an arbitrary strong monad. A single simulation transports the source logic along a ladder: it induces a morphism of the associated evidenced frames and, functorially, of the induced triposes. These passages are $2$-fully-faithful, so the three levels agree and a change of effect carries the entire higher-order program logic together with the evidence witnessing each derivation. A computationally dense simulation moreover computes a modality on the source logic, a nucleus through which the transport factors and which marks exactly the reasoning stable under the change, read off from the translation rather than postulated. This recovers known examples such as the double-negation modality of classical realizability, and examples such as sheafification arise from a modal refinement of the construction. Overall, the framework makes a change of effect a first-class object, one that can be composed, factored through its modality, and shown in cases not to exist, opening a path to transporting verified reasoning across effects.

title: Compiling Specialized GPU-Initiated Networking
summary: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.
