We present SHADOWPREFILL, which prefills the session's context on the model the router has not chosen, in capacity that instances serving normal traffic leave idle, so the next switch finds its prefix cached. SHADOWPREFILL harvests the per-iteration SLO slack of requests in flight, protects routed calls, spills shadow KV to host memory, and falls back to a cold switch whenever the shadow is incomplete. With LLMRouter routing 24 model pairs over five agentic benchmark suites, SHADOWPREFILL cuts switch-call latency by 8.5-21.4%, LLM-call latency by 3.7-17.7%, and routed token cost by 22.5-46.1%, while normal traffic keeps its SLO and energy per request rises by 0.4%.

title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
summary: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.
comment: Architecture and analysis preprint; no benchmark measurements. Companion research essay and revision notes: https://achiral.ai/research/activation-guided-graph-retrieval

title: INTENT: Out-of-Sample, Out-of-Time, and Cold-Start Evaluation on User Event Sequences
summary: Banks now train foundation models on ordered sequences of customer events such as transactions, app sessions, and authorizations. Deployed, such a model predicts forward in time, often for customers and merchants absent from training, yet each is evaluated on private data, so no two can be compared. Public benchmarks for such sequences rarely test a period the model has not seen; recommendation studies usually hold out each user's last events instead. We present INTENT (INTEraction, Novelty, and Transfer evaluation for next-action prediction), a public benchmark that scores a model in seven cells defined by whether the user, the period, and the target item appeared in training. An audit of 59 public dataset families retains five datasets; the most common defect is the lack of a calendar timestamp that orders events. No date lies within the time span of all five datasets, so each is split at its own cutoff, chosen by one rule fixed before any model is evaluated. Summed over the datasets, every cell holds at least 111,769 users. In reference results the cell determines the best model: a transformer leads on seen items after the cutoff but scores zero on new items, a variant that embeds item metadata helps mainly on MicroLens, and repeating the user's last item leads on new items in four of five datasets. This parameter-free control also shows that on three datasets most of the score lost after the cutoff reflects changed behavior rather than the model. The pipeline, the cutoff rule, and the per-cell user counts are publicly available.
comment: 4 pages + references and appendix. Accepted at the MFMB workshop at ACM ICAIF '26 (non-archival). Code: https://github.com/kthaisociety/intent

title: Contention Resolution with a Fast-but-Fickle Channel
summary: The contention-resolution problem studies how $n$ devices share a communication channel without centralized coordination. Classical models typically assume a single continuously available channel and focus on minimizing total completion time. However, modern wireless systems increasingly rely on shared spectrum, where access may be abruptly revoked by incumbent users. Motivated by this setting, we study contention resolution with two channels: a reliable slow channel and a faster channel that can be intermittently disabled by unpredictable eviction periods. Moving a batch of packets from the slow channel to the fast channel incurs a unit cost, while evictions from the fast channel impose a larger per-packet penalty. Our goal is to achieve asymptotically optimal latency while minimizing switching overhead relative to an optimal offline algorithm that knows the eviction schedule. We present Randomized Adaptive Channel Exploitation (RACE), a randomized algorithm that exploits the fast channel when available while maintaining progress on the slow channel during disruptions. When the fast channel has rate $ρ\in \bigl[Ω(\log n), O(\sqrt n)\bigr]$ and a sufficiently large constant-factor resource augmentation, RACE achieves an $O(1)$ competitive ratio for expected latency. RACE's expected switching-cost competitive ratio relative to any optimal-latency offline algorithm OPT is $O(ρ+\sqrt{n/m})$, where $m \geq 1$ is the number of fast-channel availability intervals used by OPT. We also prove a worst-case $Ω(\sqrt n)$ switching-cost competitive ratio for latency-competitive randomized algorithms, and a separate $Ω(ρ)$ switching-cost competitive-ratio lower bound. These lower bounds hold even with fixed constant-factor augmentation on both channels.

title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
summary: Users are asking language models mental health questions and are receiving answers. We audited what 41 language models recommend to users when the same clinical information reaches them from three footings: a clinician describing a patient, a caregiver describing a loved one, or a person describing themselves. Across 19 case vignettes and five questions, we collected 35,055 free-text responses, extracted every intervention named with a validated judge, and had 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale for the same cases. Models largely recommend what they rate well, with recommendation behavior differing by footing, and many models offering clinicians a consultation-style response and lay users hedged, simplified advice. When asked about recommendations for a specific intervention type, models more often named options they themselves rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached. We will release the instrument, code, and full corpus on publication as a living audit.
comment: 100 pages: 30 page main text and references, 70 page appendix. 7 figures, 2 tables. Results explorer: https://mindbench.ai/audits/interventions

title: Beyond Falsehoods 2026: Global Trends in the Regulation of Misinformation and Disinformation
summary: This report examines global legislative and regulatory responses to misinformation, disinformation, and mal-information (MDM) between 1995 and 2025. Drawing on an expanded and updated dataset of 409 coded regulatory and policy entries, including hard and soft law, policy measures, and proposed or draft instruments, it analyses their growth, geographic distribution, substantive focuses, and regulatory designs, which represent the various approaches taken against MDM, as well as early evidence of their implementation. The central finding is sustained and accelerating regulatory growth. Annual activity increased from 11 instruments in 2016 to 46 in 2023, 67 in 2024, and 71 in 2025. The number of instruments currently in force has reached 282, despite 34 measures having been repealed, withdrawn, or judicially invalidated. This growth has also been accompanied by a shift in regulatory focus. Earlier measures relied heavily on broad prohibitions of "false information," whereas more recent measures increasingly target specific harms, including deepfakes, election interference, non-consensual intimate imagery, and child safety. Regulatory responsibility is also increasingly being placed on platforms rather than solely on individual creators and users.

title: A Hoare Logic for Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
summary: Programming language researchers have developed a wide array of tools to reason about probabilistic programs, but it remains unclear how to apply these proof techniques to continuous-time stochastic processes. To bridge this gap, we propose a verification method for properties of continuous-time stochastic processes by reasoning about them as standard programs. To demonstrate our approach, we define a continuous semantics for a probabilistic imperative language $\mathrm{pWhile}^{\mathrm{dt}}$ by taking the Kuratowski limit of the standard semantics, which collects limit points of the standard program semantics as the time-step approaches zero. Then, we present a Hoare-style logic that uses loop invariants and decreasing functions to verify properties of continuous programs. To establish soundness, we identify a broad class of assertions that are preserved from the standard semantics to the continuous semantics. To demonstrate our approach, we verify properties of ten continuous-time stochastic processes modeled in $\mathrm{pWhile}^{\mathrm{dt}}$, including variants of Brownian motion and a stochastic hybrid system.

title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

title: NIFT-SQL: Customer-Supervised Table Scoring for Enterprise Text-to-SQL Retrieval
summary: Enterprise text-to-SQL starts with finding the tables a question needs, which is hard when a schema spans several databases and hundreds of cryptic tables. We ask whether models trained separately on each customer's example questions, reading only table names, column names, and declared keys, improve table retrieval. NIFT-SQL (Necessity-Informed Fusion for Text-to-SQL) fuses hybrid search over a retriever fine-tuned on the customer's questions with a fine-tuned 560M cross-encoder that scores every table for whether the query needs it, through a logistic regression fitted on held-out questions. On BEAVER, LiveSQLBench, and LiveSQLBench-Large (244 to 971 tables; four splits, three trainings), NIFT-SQL places every reference table in the top 15 for 69.2%, 89.5%, and 85.6% of test questions, against 30.4%, 41.0%, and 21.8% for hybrid search and 61.1%, 81.7%, and 70.4% for the fine-tuned retriever with the same labels. With off-the-shelf search, the cross-encoder without fine-tuning is 21 points lower. A zero-shot 8B reranker needs no labels and, routed by database, shows no resolved complete@15 difference on two collections; adding its scores as two fusion features gives a high-accuracy mode that reaches 72.4%, 92.5%, and 88.6%, ahead of the validation-selected zero-shot reranker variant on two collections, with no resolved difference on the third. Rank fusion of the two trained parts, grouped by database, shows no resolved difference from the learned fusion. Scored once on a newer BEAVER release, NIFT-SQL beats search and leads the label-matched retriever at top 8 on the synthetic test, but trails it at top 15 on real questions.

title: Scaling Taxonomy-Free Image Labeling with Generative AI: A Multimodal
summary: Providing real-time multimodal insights into images is challenging because it requires low latency, high description accuracy, and scalable solutions that are both cost-effective and efficient. For example, given a new image of an outfit, we would like to generate insights that the image depicts "earth tones" and "linen pants" and allow users to explore similar ideas along these themes. Traditional strategies to generate such insights would typically involve building taxonomies producing a golden set labeled by humans, training models on these datasets, and deploying these models for online inference services. Such workflows are constrained by fixed taxonomy, high labeling cost, limited labeling coverage in sample space, and human errors and expertise gaps in labelers. In addition, these methods are expensive and cumbersome to iterate over time. Recent trends have started exploring generative AI models for online insights, but this method suffers from long latency and prohibitive costs to support a high volume of requests or large amounts of offline labeling needs. We present Generative Labeling On Clusters (GLOC) as a solution to provide highly scalable, cost-effective, low latency, and high accuracy online image insight services. GLOC leverages highly optimized image embeddings to form image clusters that are semantically close to each other for the purpose of the type of insights, and summarizes the insights at the cluster level, which effectively generalizes to members in the cluster. At Pinterest, GLOC powers image descriptors and pivot query suggestions for Hybrid Search, which is a multimodal search service enabling users to search with both an image and a text query. Our offline and online A/B tests demonstrate that GLOC significantly outperforms previous methods, delivering improvements in quality and efficiency.
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 4th CJ Workshop at KDD 2025 (https://sites.google.com/view/kddcjworkshop2025/accepted-papers), also related: https://arxiv-org.atlassian.net/servicedesk/customer/portal/2/MOD-93955

title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
summary: Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision. Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision. Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI. Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; supplementary material as ancillary file. Code: https://github.com/valburkin/DeidSharp

title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
summary: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
summary: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.

title: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
summary: In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers. Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.
comment: 22 pages (including references), 4 figures. Submitted to SIROCCO 2027

title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product
summary: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 4-package held-out evaluation; 12,000 evaluated responses

title: Resetting-based designated information distribution
summary: For a network of $n$ nodes under random gossip dynamics, we show that by introducing the additional resetting mechanism (with rate $β$) to a designated subset of $r$ nodes, the expected sum of all node values is asymptotically equal to $\tfrac{n}{r}$ times the sum of the initial values of the $r$ designated nodes, in the small-$β$ and long-time limit. We also analyze the convergence speed to this asymptotic state and provide an approximate high-probability confidence interval for the expected sum at finite time $t$ and finite $β$. Operationally, we propose a protocol that distributes the initial node values over the designated subset evenly (up to a prescribed precision), by appropriately turning on and off the resetting dynamics. Our work not only offers insights into classical problems such as distributed computing and network control, but also serves as a potential foundation for designing quantum algorithms that prepare desired states in quantum networks using only local operations.

title: Pricing Symbolic Rules by What GNNs Leave Unlearned
summary: Symbolic knowledge (motif counts, ring counts, label constraints) is routinely added to graph neural networks (GNNs) and justified by their limited expressivity. We replace this yardstick with an exact one. The largest log-loss reduction a rule $S$ can give a model family is $I(Y;S\midσ)$ given what the family computes; every realised gain splits exactly into this term plus repaid neural debt; and for a trained network with representation $T$ the value is $I(Y;S\mid T)$, the label information training failed to extract. Rule design thus becomes rule discovery: we score candidates on the network's out-of-fold residual against calibrated permutation nulls with family-wise error control. On ZINC, discovery recovers the hidden ring term $\max(0,\ell_{\max}-6)$ of the target in three independent runs ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.001$) and beats expert cycle counts; frozen and applied to five unseen datasets it is never significantly worse than the plain network or the expert rule, and on BBBP it significantly beats both.
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables. Accepted at the GraphML Workshop (Graph Machine Learning: Foundations, Frontiers, and Applications) at the 18th Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML 2026), Melbourne, Australia

title: Frontier AI Safety and Governance 2026: Risk Understanding and Coordinated Governance
summary: Frontier AI Safety and Governance 2026: Risk Understanding and Coordinated Governance is a key outcome of the AI Safety and Governance Program of World Internet Conference Specialized Committee on AI in 2026. Drawing on the latest developments in frontier AI capabilities and applications, the report systematically examines the evolving risk landscape, analyzing key risk areas, their severity and response priorities. Building on a review of existing global governance practices and an assessment of frontier AI governance readiness, it identifies key governance gaps and weaknesses and proposes directions and practical mechanisms for coordinated responses. The report provides a reference for government departments, international organizations, businesses, research institutions and other stakeholders. It aims to strengthen the international community's understanding of and consensus on frontier AI risks, enhance preparedness and collective response capacity, and advance the safe, reliable and responsible development of frontier AI to better serve the common well-being of humanity.

title: Adapting Multi-Stage Distributed Real-Time Systems Design to Vehicular Edge Computing
summary: Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) aims to support computation-intensive applications in intelligent transportation systems while meeting stringent latency requirements. When processed remotely, applications require access to different resource types in a specific sequence, forming a multi-stage processing pipeline. This structure closely resembles multi-stage distributed applications executing across heterogeneous resources, making established multi-stage distributed real-time scheduling techniques well suited for modeling VEC systems. The resulting model accommodates diverse resource configurations and access patterns. Building on this model, we propose a joint mapping and scheduling approach that accounts for vehicle mobility and real-time constraints. The proposed heuristic extends optimal priority assignment for multi-stage systems to the VEC setting, to construct feasible schedules while minimizing local-device energy consumption and ensuring that offloaded jobs meet their deadlines. Extensive simulations show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms both a baseline based on the same delay-composition framework and a deadline decomposition-based approach.

title: Release Sooner, Expose Less: Offloading MoE Dispatch in NCCL-EP under Dual-Batch Overlap
summary: Dual-batch overlap (DBO) hides mixture-of-experts (MoE) communication behind another microbatch's computation, but only after dispatch send releases the GPU. The time dispatch send holds the GPU therefore stays exposed, while network progress after release can be hidden. We evaluate GPUDirect Async - Kernel Initiated (GDA-KI) Free Flow, an NCCL-EP research configuration that leaves WQE construction on the GPU but moves send progression to a host thread. On a GB300 NVL72 system, GDA-KI Free Flow reduces dispatch-send time relative to default GDA-KI at every operating point in the evaluated parameter sweep. An experiment that inserts a GPU delay between dispatch send and receive shows that offload increases the in-flight interval. Depending on the load, 32-96 microseconds of computation or other independent work between send and receive hides the deferred progress, leaving less exposed time than default GDA-KI. In disaggregated vLLM serving with DBO, GDA-KI Free Flow lowers median TPOT by 15-25% relative to NCCL-EP default GDA-KI and by 16-42% relative to DeepEP v1.

title: Do Machine Learning Models Predict?
summary: Machine learning (ML) models are said to predict. Philosophers draw a line between accommodation and prediction, depending on whether or not the evidence a theory succeeds on was used in constructing it. Does this distinction survive when a theory is replaced by an ML model? We argue so, yet the dividing line becomes fuzzy. Whether an output of an ML model counts as an accommodation or as a prediction hinges upon the relationship between the patterns the input instantiate and those on which the model was selected through its training. Once this relation is taken into account, most successful outputs of ML models, we suggest, bear a strong accommodation character. We further trace the consequences of our account for confirmation, novelty, and scientific realism.

title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

title: Maximizing Detection Probability in UAV Search Missions using Random-Key Optimizers
summary: This paper focuses on the stochastic and real-time constraints of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) path planning in Search and Rescue (SAR) missions. We introduce a configurable data-driven and intelligent routing architecture that combines a closed-loop probability update with the Random-Key Optimizers (RKO). Our problem is mathematically modeled as a dynamic probabilistic variant of the Open Vehicle Routing Problem (OVRP), enabling the solver to switch adaptively between two objectives, thereby balancing probability maximization and resource minimization. The framework degrades elegantly under noisy priors but not under biased ones: a systematically biased map performs about half as well as flying with no prior at all. Computational tests show that the proposed scheme is scalable and competitive with single-path scenarios in terms of solution performance and serves as a strong decision guide for intelligent planning in SAR operations in unstable environments

title: Hidden Distances: How Likert-Scale Spacing Shapes Algorithmic Voting Advice
summary: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45\% of VAA users reported following its advice. VAAs typically ask voters and candidates to respond to policy statements on a Likert scale, from ``strongly disagree'' to ``strongly agree'', and recommend candidates whose responses are closest to the voter's. Computing these distances requires assigning numbers to response options, a design choice without an empirical basis, since it is unknown how people perceive the distances between options. Here we show that this seemingly technical choice substantially changes whom voters are matched with. We parameterize the distance between ``(dis)agree'' and ``strongly (dis)agree'' relative to the distance between ``neutral'' and ``(dis)agree'' as $α$, and quantify how it changes recommendations for a popular Danish VAA. We find that moving from equidistant options to doubling this distance can change $37.7\%$ of top candidate matches and $21.9\%$ of top party matches, although no answers change. Low $α$-values favor candidates with strong positions, with some parties receiving up to $ 19.6\%$ more recommendations, while high $α$-values favor moderates. Similarly, female candidates receive fewer recommendations at low $α$ and more at high $α$-values. Our findings demonstrate that undisclosed quantification choices in algorithmic recommenders can carry considerable electoral consequences, and they call for transparency and sensitivity analysis in VAA design. As Likert-based matching also underpins dating platforms and roommate allocation systems, these implications extend well beyond elections.

title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
summary: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework. We open-source the system implementation of Evolving Infra at https://github.com/mit-han-lab/EvolvingInfra.

title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.

title: Lessons Not Learned: Why Cross-Chain Bridges Keep Losing Billions the Same Way
summary: Bridge hacks have cost billions, often without exploiting a code bug. In the cross-chain bridge hacks we catalogue from 2021 to 2026, failures of security posture, meaning how a bridge's people, code, controls and off-chain infrastructure are set up, account for 88% of reported losses since 2023, and nearly all repeat earlier failures. Code audits cannot catch these failures, so we propose a bridge security assessment rubric. It scores each bridge deployment from on-chain evidence, and a hard cap drops the score to the lowest value when a fatal risk is present. A token is only as safe as its weakest deployment if all its deployments share one backing. For attacks nobody anticipated, we show that rate limits and an emergency stop still bound the loss. We build an analyzer that applies the rubric to deployed bridges and monitors them for changes, and an agentic analyzer that runs the same checks on any bridge. Operators learn what to fix, and users can compare bridges. Our rubric's controls cut bridge hack losses 105-fold, from \$3.52B to \$33M.

title: A method to automatically discover symbolic local learning rules
summary: We present a general method for discovering symbolic local learning rules that can replace backpropagation, applicable, in principle, to any deep learning architecture and task. The method automatically discovers local loss functions specific to each layer by (1) constructing a dictionary of monomials of local tensor variables, inspired by Penrose diagram notation, (2) regressing over coefficients weighting these monomials to build layerwise polynomial losses whose gradients together minimize a target global loss. We test the method on classification, reconstruction, and self-supervised learning tasks with small multilayer networks and minimal datasets. Across all tasks, the discovered rules induce non-trivial interactions between layers, which lead to significant reductions in the corresponding global losses. Furthermore, the method selects sparse combinations of monomials, finding local rules that are more interpretable than those generated by MLP-based alternatives. The potential implications of our method range from energy-efficient deep learning to the discovery of biologically plausible learning mechanisms.

title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
summary: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

title: Optimal Proximity Black Hole Search with Programmable Matter
summary: The concept of programmable matter (PM) envisions objects composed of tiny, mobile particles capable of self-arrangement, which allows them to change shape, color, and move. We initiate the study of the Black Hole Search problem within the context of PM. The problem involves a dangerous and unnoticeable location, the black hole, that, without a trace, destroys any particle visiting it. In our setting, particles move inside a convex area embedded in a triangular grid, where one vertex is a black hole. The objective is for the particles to identify a restricted set of vertices containing the black hole while ensuring that at least one particle survives. We present an algorithm utilizing three particles capable of assuming just two colors to identify the dangerous region where the black hole resides. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this algorithm is Pareto optimal in terms of number of particles and number of colors required, and asymptotically optimal in terms of number of epochs, where an epoch refers to the minimal time window within which each particle completed an activation cycle at least once.

title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
summary: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception
summary: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total). In each scenario, FraudBench re-enacts the facts of a court case to give LLMs an opportunity, but no explicit instruction, to either misrepresent or conceal a material fact in a high-stakes commercial setting--e.g., whether to describe company-funded product testing as "independent" to customers (misrepresentation) or whether to hide unfavorable regulatory investigations from clients (concealment). We evaluate 20 LLMs across 25 experimental conditions (totaling >300,000 generations) and include a preregistered human baseline ($n_{\texttt{annotations}} = 2{,}957$, $n_{\texttt{humans}} = 996$). We score a response as fraudulent when it engages in, assists with, or recommends misrepresentation or concealment. Key findings include: (1) across LLMs, fraud rates ranged from near 0% to over 40%; (2) LLM fraud rates increased with autonomy, with overall rates of 3.0% when advising, 14.7% when drafting, and 21.4% when acting directly, without applying pressure; (3) LLMs sometimes engaged in fraud despite recognizing legal risks; (4) LLMs more often engaged in fraud by concealment than by misrepresentation; and (5) prompt-based interventions substantially affected fraud rates, with a prompt to obey the law reducing fraud rates, while prompts to maximize profits and act agentically increased fraud rates.

title: Perils and opportunities of AI for public climate services
summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative and machine-learning systems, in climate services development and provision is transforming how climate information is produced, accessed, and interpreted. AI-enabled climate services offer significant opportunities for process automation, optimisation, tailoring, and the translation of complex climate data into actionable knowledge for diverse users. However, the growing reliance on privately controlled algorithms, data infrastructures, and computing facilities raises critical concerns related to governance, transparency, equity and economic sustainability, among others. While the technical architecture of climate services increasingly relies on advanced machine learning and large-scale climate models, their legitimacy as public services may be weakened in the absence of arrangements that prioritise public value and long-lasting societal benefit over profit maximisation. The tension between the public mandate of climate services and the private nature of AI infrastructure challenges traditional notions of openness. Using a consensus-based elicitation method coupled with the PESTLE framework, we analyse the political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental risks and opportunities shaping the co-production value chain of AI-enabled climate services. We draw policy-relevant conclusions for data, model and infrastructure supporting the next generation of upstream and downstream climate services as critical applications for society. Our work presents potential and plausible challenges and benefits for a pan-European, decentralised public climate service built on sovereign AI infrastructure and open governance principles.

title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
summary: Late Chunking encodes an entire document before pooling at chunk boundaries, preserving document context in local retrieval units. Chunk-level post-training improves context-dependent retrieval, but shared context can make semantically similar same-document negatives difficult to distinguish. We study the local decision boundary between a gold chunk and its hardest sibling. Starting from InSeNT, we analyze InSeNT's within-document gradients and show that the entropy of the conditional negative allocation decreases monotonically with the scaling factor at fixed logits. We propose a two-part framework for calibrating document-local chunk boundaries. The first component adapts the discriminative scale from within-document margins, while the second exposes chunk partitions to attention during document encoding. Experiments on ConTEB and NanoBEIR show that the resulting model improves contextual chunk retrieval across the evaluated encoder settings while retaining competitive passage-level retrieval quality; ablations further characterize the distinct roles of adaptive scaling and chunk-aware routing.

title: AscendMOEA: An Ascend NPU-Accelerated Platform for Tensorized Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms
summary: Multi-objective evolutionary optimization increasingly involves large populations, expensive problem evaluations, and diverse algorithmic structures. These workloads expose the limited parallelism of loop-based implementations, while rewrites for accelerator execution can alter selection order, tie handling, and population updates. AscendMOEA is presented as a scalable platform that executes multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) on Huawei Ascend neural processing units (NPUs) and conventional central processing units (CPUs). The platform represents the decision vectors, objectives, constraints, and auxiliary states as tensors and provides reusable interfaces for algorithms, problems, population operators, quality indicators, monitoring, and repeated experiments. Dense computations are executed in batches, such as dominance, distance, variation, and problem-evaluation calculations. Short recurrences with causal dependencies retain their prescribed order and consume precomputed tensor results, which preserves the behavior of the original algorithms. AscendMOEA contains 18 algorithms, 155 benchmark and application problems, 19 public operator interfaces, and 11 quality indicators. Experiments on eight Ascend NPUs and 192 physical CPU cores evaluate operator throughput, end-to-end runtime, memory consumption, numerical agreement, and implementation ablation. Tensorized operators obtain a median acceleration of 1.58 times on the NPU. At large population scales, complete algorithms achieve a median acceleration of 5.76 times while retaining the recorded quality indicators. Moreover, the results identify the workload scale and ordered computation that determine whether accelerator execution is beneficial. AscendMOEA is open-sourced at https://github.com/dqlme/AscendMOEA.

title: ShiftCache: Fast and Exact Indel Effect Prediction by Reusing Shifted Reference Encodings
summary: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7$\times$ faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1$\times$ faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6$\times$ faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic. On an A6000, every checked output of the default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs matches dense execution within an absolute and relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$. With larger tile batches, with Enformer or on an H100, a small fraction of values exceeds this tolerance.

title: Two-Tier Task Offloading for Satellite-Assisted Marine Networks: A Hybrid Stackelberg-Bargaining Game Approach
summary: The proliferation of maritime activities has spurred the emergence of numerous computation-intensive and delay-sensitive marine applications and services. Given the inherent rationality, selfish nature, and limited computational abilities of marine devices, devising effective strategies to incentivize their participation in task processing become a critical challenge. In this paper, we investigate the satellite-assisted marine multi-access edge computing (MEC) and propose a two-tier task offloading scheme through a hybrid Stackelberg-Bargaining game approach to enhance offloading efficiency and maximize the utility of marine devices. Specifically, for the underwater acoustic communication, we consider the scenario where multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), managed by maritime autonomous surface ships (MASSs), upload their collected data using non-orthogonal multiple access(NOMA) to optimize channel utilization. For the data transmission above the sea surface, we consider the scenario where a low earth orbit satellite (LEOS) functions as a space edge server to provide computing services, and MASS offloads workloads to LEOS through frequency division multiple access(FDMA) to prevent co-channel interference. we define the utility of AUVs, MASSs and LEOSs, and model the offloading process between AUVs and MASSs as a Stackelberg game, while representing the offloading interaction between MASSs and LEOSs as a Bargaining game. Additionally, we propose efficient algorithms to optimize AUV offloading strategies and MASS pricing strategies, while refining the bidding strategies for both MASSs and LEOSs. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms significantly outperform benchmark schemes in achieving optimal solutions.

title: CHO-Bench: How Do Context Hints Affect Ad Rankings in LLM Advertising?
summary: LLM advertising selects advertisements based on user conversations, where user needs may extend beyond explicit product searches. ChatGPT Ads allows advertisers to provide natural-language context hints describing what they offer, who may find it useful, and when it may be useful, as additional information for ranking advertisements across diverse user conversations. However, how to effectively construct these hints remains unclear. We formulate Context Hint Optimization (CHO) as the problem of constructing context hints to improve an advertisement's ranking under a given budget. Drawing on established marketing frameworks, we develop seven context hint generation strategies covering What, Who, and When, along with a Unified strategy that combines all seven dimensions. We introduce CHO-Bench and conduct over 1.19 million paired evaluations across five datasets using embedding-based and LLM-based rankers. Our results show that context hints improve advertisement rankings under the evaluated offline rankers. While individual strategies achieve similar average gains and Unified offers no consistent advantage, strategy differences become more pronounced under specific generation-ranking configurations, with embedding-based and LLM-based rankers favoring different information dimensions. Increasing the hint budget further improves rankings with diminishing marginal gains. These findings establish an offline benchmark for studying ad-side ranking optimization in LLM advertising and highlight opportunities for model-specific hint selection and budget-aware generation and aggregation.

title: Attention at Absolute Zero
summary: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.

title: Properties of Public Announcements as Operators: Commutativity, Monotonicity, Idempotence, Fixed Points, and Stabilization
summary: For each formula $\varphi$, we introduce the public announcement operator $U_\varphi$, which maps every model to its updated model under the public announcement of $\varphi$. We then study its algebraic and dynamic properties with a particular focus on commutativity, monotonicity, idempotence, fixed points, and stabilization. Among many results, we show the following. First, monotonicity of $U_\varphi$ is characterized by a family of preservation conditions and equivalence to an existential formula. Second, there exists a formula that achieves every nonzero ordinal as a stabilization rank---the first stage at which a model stabilizes---of some model. Finally and unexpectedly, extinction of every model under iterated announcements of $\varphi$ is equivalent to common unknowability, being always informative when true, and a fixed point view of the Moore sentence. Over S5, those are further equivalent to common unbelievability and being always informative. Other results include characterizations of commutativity and strong commutativity, idempotence as success, properties of fixed points, and finite and $ω$-stabilization. For analysis, we use PAL (state elimination) and BPAL (arrow elimination), clarifying their subtle differences.

title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.

title: Developing a Street View Imagery Processing Pipeline for Building-Level Vacant House Assessment
summary: Street view imagery (SVI) is widely used to audit urban environments remotely. Automated assessments usually assume that each image shows the target building clearly. In practice, an image may lack task-relevant evidence or show a neighboring house. If this goes unchecked, a model's score cannot show whether it judged the correct building. We present a reproducible SVI processing pipeline that makes image suitability and target identity explicit and checkable. We apply it to vacant house assessment in South Korea, using 10,311 images of 1,609 detached-house parcels. Task-suitability filtering adapts its criteria to image composition and administrative area. This keeps coverage even across areas. While keeping as many images as a single uniform filter, our filtering left 101 more parcels with a usable image. Target-house alignment identifies the parcel's house from camera metadata and parcel boundaries. It needs no building footprints or additional training. Alignment matched human labels for 85.6% of images, compared with 79.8% for the best simple rule. In vacancy classification, filtering and alignment raised AUROC from 0.684 to 0.719, but marking a different house in the same image still gave 0.709. Grad-CAM showed that the model often looked at areas outside the target house. Image suitability, target identification, and model evidence are therefore separate problems, and scores alone do not resolve them. Recording which images were used and which house was selected lets reviewers verify each assessment and can support human virtual audits.

title: Multi-Modal Agricultural Document Understanding at the DAGRI Task
summary: Agricultural documents, such as prefectural technical reports and crop calendars, are critical knowledge resources. However, their complex table layouts, significant variations in document length, and dense multi-modal elements pose substantial challenges for automated understanding. To address these issues, the NTCIR-19 DAGRI (Data Analytics for aGRicultural Information) task introduced three subtasks focusing on different dimensions of document intelligence. In the Table Information Extraction (TableIE) task, we developed a multi-stage pipeline combining structure-preserving parsing via MinerU, region-adaptive segmentation for long documents, and a dual-modal (vision-text) extraction strategy for complex work schedules. This approach achieved first place with an exact match score of 0.6566. For Multi-Table Multi-Hop Question Answering (MTMH-QA) over interrelated JSON tables, we adopted an agentic search framework utilizing DCI-Agent to iteratively explore directories via bash commands, reinforced by a cross-model validation mechanism. This yielded a revised accuracy of 0.8444, initially ranked first. In the Figure and Table Question Answering (FiT-QA) task, which requires comprehending single large composite images, we implemented a dual-modal VLM pipeline enhanced by deterministic answer normalization, securing the highest BLEU score. Together, our system effectively addresses regional structural variations, dynamic cross-file evidence discovery, and multi-modal alignment, providing a robust framework for complex agricultural document understanding.

title: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers with Graph Computing Accelerators
summary: Solving large sparse linear systems by Gaussian elimination is a challenging computational task due to the introduction of non-zero elements, or fill-in. Practitioners use heuristics such as the nested dissection reordering algorithm to try to reduce fill-in. In practice, reordering codes do not achieve the same parallel scaling as factorization, nor can they exploit AVX instructions or GPUs. Thus, reordering can be the primary runtime bottleneck in large-scale computer-aided engineering applications. We consider the use of a novel accelerator, the UpDown system, to accelerate the METIS multilevel nested dissection reordering algorithm. The UpDown system is designed for a broad class of graph computing and irregular algorithms. We report results for small-scale UpDown systems that will be available commercially in 2027, using validated simulation and FPGA emulation platforms. Our findings indicate that small UpDown systems can speed up METIS by two-orders of magnitude versus a single CPU. Compared to ParMETIS on hundreds of MPI ranks, we anticipate the same small UpDown systems offer speedups of 4 - 7, providing the potential to significantly speed finite element simulations

title: DeFSM: Robust and Efficient Decentralization of Federated Submodular Maximization
summary: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.

title: OverlapAdvisor: Modeling and Adapting Computation-Communication Overlap for Distributed MoE Serving
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference with expert parallelism (EP) relies on All-to-All communication, making computation-communication overlap strategies critical for achieving high performance. However, no strategy is universally optimal. Across 103 production configurations, varying input lengths, and four hardware platforms, we observe that the fastest strategy shifts based on model shape, EP degree, input length, and hardware. Since no strategy dominates more than 80.6% of configurations, configuration-aware selection is necessary. In this work, we propose OverlapAdvisor, which models overlap stages using two granularities to capture computation-communication dependencies. OverlapAdvisor builds a unified performance model, accounting for deviations from peak compute, memory, and communication performance across workloads and hardware. This model enables launch-time, configuration-aware strategy selection within two serving engines. We conduct experiments on four MoE models (30B-235B) against three baselines, utilizing SGLang and vLLM. At the kernel level, OverlapAdvisor achieves 1.16x average and 1.59x maximum speedups, with a prediction MAPE of 3.3%-15.9%. In SGLang and vLLM, it improves end-to-end throughput up to 31.7%. Its granularity-guided optimizations further achieve median speedups of 1.10x for DeepEP-v1 and 1.22x for FlashMoE.

title: AI and Mathematical Work on Mastodon: Attention, Topics, and Target-Specific Evaluations
summary: How does a mathematical community discuss AI on a federated social platform? We study 24,920 public posts from January--September 2026 by 272 accounts in a fixed roster of 1,002 Mastodon accounts whose profiles indicate mathematical research or study. LLM-assisted extraction identifies 1,191 AI-for-mathematics posts by 101 accounts. Their share of all posts rises from 1.1\% in January to 11.5\% in September, with contributing accounts increasing from 10 to 59. We represent discussion through linked target--aspect--stance triples, separating what is discussed from the property assessed and the author's evaluation. From July to September, capability and usefulness decline as a share of related discussion, while social and institutional concerns increase; changing contributors account for much of the latter shift. Among 38 accounts evaluating both technical quality or utility and communication, credit, or verification procedures, the procedural negative-component fraction is 19.4 percentage points higher on average (95\% account-bootstrap interval: 3.8--35.1). Matching targets within posts gives a similar direction. Repeated extraction varies substantially at the level of individual triples, although replacing the repeated sample preserves the aggregate contrast. Around OpenAI's October 6 mathematics release, related-post share rises from 9.6\% to 13.6\%, and contributing accounts increase from 13 to 28. Post-release discussion includes appreciation of the results' potential mathematical value and applications alongside criticism of promotion centered on result counts, limited methodological disclosure, and verification arrangements.

title: Exploiting Native Hardware Heterogeneity: Custom GPSIMD Operators for Accelerating Emerging LLM Memory on AWS Trainium
summary: Emerging memory modules of large language models, such as Engram in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, mix irregular integer work (a 64-bit n-gram hash and a sparse table lookup) with dense computation (a GEMM and a gate). When deploying on a GPU-FPGA system, we can disaggregate operations to different devices for Engram to speed up by 5.9$\times$. AWS Trainium provides a similar heterogeneity natively: each Trainium NeuronCore pairs dense engines with a customizable GPSIMD Engine, and all engines share the on-chip SBUF. However, the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) exposes the GPSIMD cores only through fixed built-in instructions, and the official GPSIMD custom-operator toolchain does not support Trainium 2 or 3 and cannot be used with NKI. In this work, we build a toolchain that compiles C++ custom operators for the GPSIMD cores and injects them into the compiled NEFF from the NKI kernel on Trainium 3, expanding the customizability of GPSIMD with the current software stack. Over a hand-optimized NKI baseline of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, two GPSIMD operators speed up the n-gram hashing by 1.79$\times$ at decode, the table retrieval by up to 4.95$\times$, and the whole Engram computation by up to 1.14$\times$.

title: Compile-Gated Lean Proof Refactoring with Enterprise Agent Practices: A Model per Step under a US\$3 Cap, Followed by Programmatic Rewrite Rules
summary: Our closed-track entry (Arena username Vexorium-Agent) scored 86.31 points on the final board (L = 77.07, H = 81.86, Z = 100) over the 60 final problems, against 33.33 for the reference proofs, 8th at the deadline (top: 92.57), for US\$166.33 at list prices with every call counted (per problem: mean US\$2.772, at most US\$2.874; US\$3 cap). Three practices carry the entry. First, each paid stage runs the model that measured best per dollar for it among the 9 we tested in our own harness: GPT-6.1 Sol the early sessions, GPT-6.1 Terra the later ones and the tail at 70% of Sol's cost per turn, and Gemini 4 Argon the review and repair; Sol also runs the style rewrite. Second, what our development and research runs learned ships as compiler-checked programmatic rewrite rules rather than prompt text (+0.93 points from rules fixed before the release; +0.26 and +0.30, in sample, from passes built or switched on after the release). Third, every call is recorded and reviewed before each change (all 9 board scores came within -0.063 to +0.015 points of our meter's prediction). The harness, gate and many of these rules also serve our open-track entry. We report the full bill and the spread of three runs.
comment: 20 pages. Technical report of team Vexorium-Agent for the closed track of the Lean Refactor Arena, a competition at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding

title: Proactive Dimension-Adaptive Denoising for Graph Collaborative Filtering via Representation Coherence
summary: Implicit feedback in recommender systems contains noisy interactions (e.g., accidental clicks, impulse purchases) that propagate through user-item graphs and contaminate learned representations. Existing explicit denoising methods uniformly rely on training loss to estimate interaction reliability. However, loss is a fundamentally passive signal: it detects noise only after it has caused prediction errors, and it is heavily confounded by training stage, negative sampling, and hard positives. We propose Noise-aware Dimension Learning (NDL), a proactive dimension-adaptive denoising framework. NDL introduces Representation Coherence Detection (RCD), which evaluates the coherence between an interaction representation and the user's historical preference centroid in embedding space, providing an active noise signal independent of loss. RCD and the loss signal are fused via activity-aware weighting (active users rely more on coherence while cold-start users automatically fall back to loss), and the fused estimate drives an interaction-level dimension-adaptive mask that limits the effective representation capacity of unreliable interactions. A lightweight contrastive regularizer further improves embedding uniformity, stabilizing the geometry on which RCD discriminates. On three public benchmarks NDL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art denoising methods, lifting Recall@5 by +17.95% on Amazon-book, +12.33% on Yelp, and +5.63% on MovieLens-1M over the strongest baseline DAR; the core variant without contrastive learning already surpasses DAR on sparser datasets, confirming representation coherence as the primary driver of these gains. NDL is confined to the training loop and is serving-compatible with LightGCN-based production pipelines, adding no online latency or parameters at inference time. Code: https://github.com/GordonDongZHAO/NDL

title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
summary: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.

title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
summary: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable.
