An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

title: ArcadeDB in Python: An In-Process Multi-Model Database
summary: Some Python workflows need transactional reads and writes over documents, traversals over a graph, and similarity search over vector embeddings. In practice these are split across separate systems (a document store, a graph engine, and a vector index), and the data is copied between them and kept consistent by application code. ArcadeDB is an open-source multi-model database engine, written in Java, that supports all three access patterns and can be embedded in a host process. We present arcadedb-embedded, a Python package that runs ArcadeDB inside the Python process via JPype, using a Java Runtime Environment bundled in the wheel. One pip install gives a database with documents, a property graph, and vector search, and needs no Java installation. Query results can be returned as Python lists, NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames, or Arrow tables. We demonstrate a hybrid retrieval workflow that chains vector search, SQL filtering, and graph traversal over one dataset. We benchmark arcadedb-embedded against SQLite, DuckDB, LadybugDB, and Chroma, and report its costs.
comment: 12 pages. Published in the SciPy Proceedings 2026 (Proceedings of the 25th Python in Science Conference), https://proceedings.scipy.org/articles/fwvt2525

title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
summary: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.
comment: Extended abstract, UniReps workshop at NeurIPS 2026

title: zkARc: Succinctly Verifiable Proofs for Neurosymbolic Natural Language Formalization and Verification
summary: Autonomous agents increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of users, but ordinary middleware guardrails do not provide cryptographic proof that a policy was actually enforced. Their verdicts leave counterparties dependent on the operator unless they repeat the checks themselves, potentially exposing sensitive policies and inputs. We present zkARc, a modular proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of Automated Reasoning checks (ARc) in an independent, succinctly verifiable zero-knowledge proof. ARc is a neurosymbolic system that translates natural language policies into formal logic and verifies AI-generated content against them using SMT solvers. zkARc certifies the planner's output, the policy's formalization, the action's formalization and both solver queries. The receipt binds these computations to the exact action received and, under the stated assumptions, reveals no additional information about private policies and intermediate model values beyond the declared public information and verdict. This lets a third party check the claimed policy enforcement without re-running the pipeline or trusting the operator. We prove completeness, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge for the composed receipt under explicit assumptions. An implementation on Qwen2-0.5B enforces a spending policy end to end, approving two purchases and denying a third. A full receipt, which also proves model inference, takes about an hour to issue with CPU-only proving and verifies in under a minute, and the solver proof alone is 88 KiB and verifies in 0.3 seconds.

title: tok: a textual concrete syntax of BPMN and DMN for humans and AI agents
summary: tok is a plain-text notation for Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0.2 process models and Decision Model and Notation (DMN) 1.5 decisions. One engine checks a tok document against both standards, compiles the document to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The paper classifies the notation as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels and reports one study. A tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML of 893 files exported by 37 tools and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported. The checker signals 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults, against 85.8% for the XML Schema with bpmnlint. Four language models new to tok write valid tok from a one-page reference for 85.7 to 100% of 87 process descriptions from two datasets and valid BPMN XML for every description, and the strongest model writes tok with 25% and 19% fewer tokens than BPMN XML. As agents with a lean skill and one checker tool, the models write valid tok for 97.6 to 100% of the descriptions, the strongest model spends 21% and 14% fewer tokens on tok than on BPMN XML, and a skill which sends the model to read the reference through a tool costs 1.7 to 2.8 times the tokens of the lean skill. Of 47 event logs simulated from public models, 44 fit their source models, and tok imports every model discovered from the logs.

title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.

title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
summary: Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent. We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost. Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.

title: CORE: Coarse-to-Fine Search with Context Management for Deep Research
summary: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent's context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE, a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus-CM), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

title: Tasteply: Externalizing Stable and Situational Preference as Manipulable Spatial Objects
summary: Most recommender systems treat user preferences as a single signal to infer and optimize, yet human preferences are a mix of a stable preference and situational preferences that turn on and off depending on context. Through Tasteply, we externalize this preference structure as manipulable spatial objects. Tasteply represents each situational preference as an attractor and the stable preference as an underlying global field. Users can adjust their feed by moving around the space and adjusting the strength of the global field, turning the preference structure that remains latent within the model into something they can see and act on directly to steer the recommendation algorithm. Through an exploratory study (N=5), we found that this spatial control was effective, along with its limits and future direction as a means of manipulating preference-based recommendations.

title: Reliability-Aware Z-Grammars and Z-Automata over a Credible-Grade Semiring
summary: Fuzzy grammars and weighted automata usually attach to each word a single grade, which records how strongly the word is generated but not how far that record can be trusted. We study weighted grammars and finite automata whose weights are scalar grade-reliability pairs inspired by Z-numbers. Sequential composition multiplies both components, while aggregation selects a derivation by its credible grade, the product of grade and reliability, with ties resolved by grade. On the canonical carrier, in which the weights of zero grade or zero reliability are identified with zero, the resulting structure is a commutative selective semiring, isomorphic to a subsemiring of a lexicographically ordered product, and its credible-grade projection is a homomorphism onto the Viterbi semiring. We compare several alternative combination rules and identify the carriers on which the relevant algebraic laws hold. Standard results on weighted automata then yield a rational characterization and closure properties. We prove that positive credible-grade cuts and selected-run reliability filters of finite automata are regular and effectively constructible for rational weights and thresholds, and we exhibit distinctions that the scalar projection cannot see: a reliability filter that no scalar reweighting of the same one-state automaton implements, nonmonotonicity under the addition of runs, and an unambiguous automaton with no deterministic equivalent although its scalar projection is deterministic. A count-based example illustrates an attestation penalty for grammar rules. The construction concerns scalar pairs, and its extension to arbitrary fuzzy-valued Z-numbers remains open.

title: Projection-Free Gradient Tracking Neurodynamic for Distributed Nonnegative Sparse Optimization
summary: This paper proposes a continuous-time, projection-free neurodynamic system based on gradient tracking for distributed nonnegative sparse optimization. Unlike traditional methods, our approach avoids projecting states onto the feasible set. Instead, it employs gradient tracking to estimate average gradients under heterogeneous costs, coupling primal and dual dynamics such that feasibility and sparsity emerge naturally from the equilibrium conditions. The system ensures unique solutions through a locally Lipschitz vector field and guarantees that every equilibrium corresponds to an exact KKT point. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees for convex objectives through three distinct analytical layers. These include a centralized kernel rate, a computable distributed rate derived from Jacobian analysis without restrictive stability assumptions, and a global exponential stability proof based on Lur'e system theory. Our analysis quantitatively separates these layers, revealing that the convergence rate is primarily limited by graph sparsity and remains robust to variations in momentum time scales. Numerical experiments on strongly convex quadratic problems validate the theoretical rates, demonstrate effective active set recovery, and show that the system maintains stable tail convergence rates even under strong local heterogeneity.

title: MEMOIR: A Training-Free Memory Lifecycle for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents require memory systems that preserve useful information across sessions and retrieve it when needed. Existing systems treat these as separate problems: memories are written prospectively with static importance scores that are never revised after use. This creates two coupled failure modes: consolidation can silently destroy evidence that future queries require, while retrieval continues to favor stale memories. We propose MEMOIR (Memory Evidence via Merge-certified, Online Importance Revision), a training-free memory lifecycle that unifies judge-gated consolidation with retrospective attribution. Before compressing memory, screening gates test whether answer-relevant evidence is preserved. After each query, attribution estimates which retrieved memories supported the answer and updates their retrieval priority. A UCB-style exploration bonus additionally encourages retrieval of under-exposed memories, reducing the risk that frequently retrieved memories crowd out useful but less-seen evidence. On 1,905 deduplicated LoCoMo QA pairs, the full retrieval stack improves evidence recall@5 by 11.92 percentage points over bare cosine, with confidence-gated feedback adding 1.50 points overall without reference answers or reranker training; a deployment-unavailable oracle adds 1.84 points overall and 8.05 points on multi-hop. Judge-gated merge changes the recall of text-based evidence from 58.82% to 59.08%, reduces the active store by 1.42%, and incurs 0 observed losses in 100 independently audited merges, with a one-sided 95% upper loss-rate bound of 2.95%. Together, these results outline a practical deployment path: no additional LLM call on the online write path, with merge screening confined to periodic offline consolidation. The lifecycle reduces to one principle: attribute usefulness after use, and screen for preservation before compression.

title: When Does Blockwise Additivity Break? Diagnosing and Repairing the Additive Assumption in Distillation-Based Architecture Search
summary: Blockwise distillation methods for architecture search, such as DNA, DONNA, LANA and Puzzle, score each candidate replacement block in isolation and combine the scores additively. We ask at which budgets this additivity assumption fails, whether fine-tuning repairs the failure, what diagnoses it, and how it can be repaired cheaply. On DeiT-S, DeiT-B, Swin-T and Qwen2.5-0.5B with seven latency budgets each, an additive integer program trails a pairwise interaction-aware program after fine-tuning by at most 1.6 top-1 points on ImageNet-1k at the mildest budgets, but by up to 17.5 points, and a factor of 1.9 in perplexity, at aggressive ones. After 10,000 fine-tuning steps 3.3-9.9 points remain on DeiT, whereas on Swin-T the gap shrinks to at most about 1.8 points within 500 steps. In a learning-rate sweep with the standard 2,000 steps, 6.0-10.7 points remain on DeiT when each method's rate is chosen by its evaluation-set accuracy. An intervention that keeps the block library and only forbids more than two removals in any three adjacent layers shrinks the DeiT gap from 5.8-17.5 to 0.7-5.2 points, mostly by improving the additive solution: adjacent removals are a major failure pattern. Splitting the additivity error into a metric and a functional part, relative to additive logit changes, indicates where a cheap logit-sum predictor can be trusted. A hybrid search that ranks moves with this predictor and measures only the best needs no pair measurements and, after Holm adjustment, is significantly better than the pairwise program in 10 of 14 ImageNet-1k settings, with no statistically significant losses. An ablation shows that its ranking helps except at the most aggressive DeiT-B budget, where the predictor misleads and random ranking or ten-times-costlier evolution does better.
comment: v2: added Swin-T and Qwen2.5-0.5B experiments, run-length interventions, ablations; restructured

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions
summary: Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds; proof irrelevance in conversion erases, at the kernel level, how a claim was established. A persistent knowledge store, by contrast, must retain that record: who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions. This volume presents the theory of Eigenius---a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions---and develops its metatheory from that requirement. The kernel theory is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative universe of propositions, inductive families, and an intensional identity type. Proof irrelevance is an axiom with an explicit witness rather than a conversion rule, so proofs of a proposition are provably equal yet remain distinct terms. Definitional equality is joinability under an orthogonal rewriting system---confluent, injective on type formers, and decidable by a type-free test---while a separate subsumption judgment covers universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant function types, and declared class inclusions. We prove consistency via a set-theoretic model; develop a justification logic over the kernel's propositions to track evidence and support; organize environments as an institution so that store extensions are signature morphisms and external verdicts enter via comorphisms; formulate a typed knowledge-graph theory with records, classes, and refinements; and prove the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation, and bidirectional type checking relative to termination. A Lean 4 formalization accompanies the volume.

title: Frustration-freeness is decidable but unprovable
summary: The frustration-free property is valuable in quantum many-body systems, which states that its ground states simultaneously minimize all local interaction terms, even when these terms act on overlapping degrees of freedom. Prominent examples include the AKLT model and Kitaev's toric code model, which serve as paradigmatic models of symmetry-protected topological phases and topological order, respectively. A fundamental question is whether a given Hamiltonian is frustration-free for all system sizes. Here we establish two seemingly contradictory results concerning this decision problem. First, we prove that frustration-freeness is decidable for any fixed local Hilbert space dimension. Specifically, there exists a finite, Hamiltonian-independent system-size cutoff such that frustration-freeness at this cutoff size guarantees frustration-freeness at all system sizes. Second, on the other hand, we also show that there exists a frustration-free Hamiltonian whose frustration-freeness cannot be proved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC). We reconcile these seemingly contradictory results by showing that the cutoff, although finite for each local Hilbert space dimension, is uncomputable as a function of that dimension. Our findings reveal an unexpected fundamental distinction between decidability and provability arising in quantum many-body physics.

title: Degree profiles of uniform polynomial consequences: Linear lower bounds for Nullstellensatz and Polynomial Calculus
summary: This paper proves asymptotically optimal linear degree lower bounds for Nullstellensatz and Polynomial Calculus, yielding a four-way polynomial-versus-exponential proof-size classification for uniform polynomial consequences over fields of positive characteristic. The size bounds use full, explicit coefficient lists, including zeros. Apart from a fixed finite initial range, exactly one of four cases occurs: $\mathrm T_1$, bounded degree; $\mathrm T_2$, degree at least linear in the universe size $n$; $\mathrm T_3$, constant degree on some residue classes and at least linear degree on the others; or $\mathrm T_4$, infinitely many recurring finite degrees, with bounded-degree subsequences and finite $Ω(n)$ peaks at arbitrarily large sizes. Thus the size patterns are polynomial bounds, exponential lower bounds, a periodic mixture, or polynomial subsequences with finite exponential peaks, respectively. Underivable targets have degree $\infty$, and both proof systems assign the same type. The result strengthens my 2008--2009 refutation classification and extends it to uniform consequences. The proof uses degree-preserving lifting with onset and period bounds linear in the degree. A common $p$-adic hardness spectrum describes the four types topologically. Distinguishing any two types is undecidable already for refutations. The linear degree bounds, four-way classification and pairwise undecidability results have been formalised and verified in Lean. The Lean formalisation, verification records and an accompanying tutorial are available in the supporting materials (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23965838).
comment: 78 pages. Tutorial, Lean formalisation and verification records: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23965838

title: A Complete Equational Theory for Quantum Circuits with Generalized Control
summary: Controlled subcircuits are commonplace in quantum algorithms as they represent the quantum analogue of branching statements (if then). We introduce a generalization of controlled subcircuits in the form of a binary operation which sends pairs of unitary quantum circuits to a generalized controlled operation, whose semantics are based on matrix exponentials and logarithms. The family of quantum circuits with generalized controlled operations and circuit exponentiation is denoted HQC for Hierarchical Quantum Circuits. We formalize HQC as a modified prop category using a novel category-theoretic construction, and provide a sound and complete equational theory for diagrammatic reasoning in HQC.

title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
summary: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
summary: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; https://github.com/BjBodner/amm-optimizer).

title: Monadically Dependent Graph Classes Have Almost Bounded Merge-Width
summary: A graph class $\mathcal{C}$ is monadically dependent if one cannot interpret all graphs in vertex-colored graphs from $\mathcal{C}$ using a fixed formula of first-order logic. We prove that every monadically dependent graph class has almost bounded merge-width, thereby confirming a conjecture of the first and the last author [STOC '25]. Our proof is algorithmic and the witnessing decompositions in the form of merge sequences can be computed in nearly-cubic time. This is a step towards the proof of fixed-parameter tractability of model checking first-order logic on monadically dependent graph classes, which is achieved in a companion paper.

title: The Logic of Emergence
summary: ``Emergence'' refers to the fact that different mathematical languages and theories seem to be required to describe scientific theories that operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Highly circumscribed, special cases of emergence have been investigated using many different formal tools, including coarse-graining (over space and / or time), renormalization, dimension reduction, broken symmetry, and various formulations of causality. Here we extend the mathematics of model theory to unify and extend these earlier investigations. As a preliminary application of our framework, we investigate canonical examples of emergence, including the emergence of genetics from chemistry, of psychology from neurobiology, and of different forms of collective behavior from the laws governing their constituent parts. By exploiting the power of model theory we also uncover many aspects of emergence that were previously obscured. In particular, we uncover some of the rich hierarchical structure that relates different scientific fields. For example, we show that scientific fields can be related via a collection of multiple partial orders, all defined over the same set. On the other hand, under an alternative relation among scientific fields, one which allows cycles, we show that it is possible that the set of all of scientific fields must collapse into a single scientific field. Going forward, these investigations point to the formal tools that might need to be developed in order to arrive at a deeper understanding of this emergent hierarchy of scientific reality.

title: From Certified Pairs to a Certified Hub: Reasoner-Checked Crosswalks for the Information Exchange Standard
summary: A national digital twin was conceived as an ecosystem of twins connected through mappings to a common foundation, but the roadmap that promises to confirm those mappings are valid never says what valid means. We give the test a precise form, coherence and conservativity of the merged ontology, borrowed from logic-based alignment repair, and apply it to the Information Exchange Standard (IES), first pair by pair and then to whole hubs. Crosswalks from IES into thirteen ontologies across seven sector groups, anchored on the building ontologies BOT, Brick, and SAREF4BLDG, pass through separate stages of matching, human review, certification of each SKOS correspondence against the two class hierarchies, and reasoning with HermiT. Pair by pair, the stages catch different failures: certification alone removed all 526 conservativity violations of the raw crosswalks, review alone left 73, and together they made eleven of twelve overlapping pairs coherent and conservative. Pairwise certification does not compose. Merging the three certified building crosswalks into one hub made five Brick classes unsatisfiable, through a homonym between the IES and Brick notions of a floor that only BOT's disjointness axioms expose; rejecting that one row gave a coherent and conservative hub that entails 290 cross-ontology links nobody wrote down. The core hub is inconsistent before any crosswalk is added, because two published standards, the Open Energy Ontology and BFO 2020, contradict each other; with either one left out it is coherent and conservative. A hub, not a pair, is the unit an ecosystem of twins has to certify.

title: SpikePose: Lightweight Video Human Pose Estimation
summary: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.

title: From Admission to Retention: Predicting Durable Offspring in Quality-Diversity Search
summary: Automated failure discovery can be framed as a diversity problem: the objective is to expose distinct ways a system fails rather than a single critical adversarial case. Yet uniform parent sampling provides no way to allocate search effort toward individuals likely to produce durable archive contributions. We study this credit assignment problem in an unstructured Quality-Diversity (QD) archive, testing whether signals available before an individual has reproduced distinguish offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later. Across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, the same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions. In particular, lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover. Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems (EvoRobust)

title: Timed Games under Environmental Interference with Real-Time Objectives
summary: Classical Timed Games formulations may be unsuitable, or require substantial modeling effort, to capture complex interaction patterns between a controller and its surrounding environment, in which non-determinism must be resolved after the controller has chosen which action to perform. In this paper, we develop the theory of Timed CLTLoc Games (TCGs), a Timed Game variant designed to facilitate the modeling of such patterns. Unlike classical Timed Games formulations, TCGs partition locations rather than transitions, and use Constraint Linear Temporal Logic over clocks (CLTLoc) to specify the controller's objectives. We develop algorithms for solving TCGs and synthesizing winning controller strategies for games whose objectives include formal properties such as reachability and safety. For reachability objectives, our synthesis algorithm yields winning controller strategies that minimize the number of moves required to reach a goal state. Solving reachability TCGs is EXPTIME-complete, matching the complexity of solving reachability Timed Games. All of our algorithms operate backwards and are implemented in our C++ region-based library TARZAN, leveraging OpenMP for efficient parallelization. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of TARZAN.

title: Multi-Resident Data Association in Smart Homes via MDP Modeling and Behavior Cloning
summary: Ambient sensors offer a privacy-preserving solution for activity recognition in smart homes, yet they face a critical challenge in multi-resident environments known as Data Association, which aims to identify the resident triggering a specific anonymous sensor event. Existing approaches fundamentally fail to maintain global consistency by often yielding conflicting associations for silent residents. Additionally, these methods frequently suffer from severe trajectory fragmentation caused by the ontological mismatch of applying continuous physical motion models to discrete logical behaviors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that reformulates data association as a sequential decision-making task within a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We solve the defined MDP via Behavior Cloning (BC) to avoid complex reward engineering by directly learning from expert demonstrations. We instantiate the policy using two complementary architectures, including a lightweight Transformer that treats association as a multi-label classification task over linearized event histories, and a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM) that reformulates the problem as conditional text generation to leverage pre-trained semantic knowledge. Extensive evaluations on three diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in resolving concurrent multi-resident events. Furthermore, the LLM-based policy shows preliminary cross-environment transfer potential under benchmark settings, while its robustness in real deployments still requires further validation.

title: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
summary: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.

title: Executable Specifications in Transition Algebra
summary: Transition Algebra can be viewed as an extension of many-sorted first-order logic by borrowing essential features from dynamic logic. This leads us to new, more expressive sentences that include transitions labelled with actions, which are built from terms using union, composition, and iteration operators. We define a suitable notion of Horn clause, develop a system of proof rules for reasoning about clauses, and subsequently show that the proof system is sound and complete. We then introduce a rewriting relation based on Horn clauses, capturing transitions along established paths expressed as actions. This rewriting relation is naturally extended to a narrowing procedure for solving queries, thereby laying foundation for logic programming in Transition Algebra. As usual, soundness for both rewriting and narrowing is straightforward, whereas completeness requires additional conditions. Finally, we provide a prototype tool that demonstrates the practical aspects and shows the effectiveness of the proposed method.

title: Mobility-Aware Mobile Edge Computing for Energy-Balanced Data Collection in IoT-Enabled Underwater Sensor Networks
summary: Underwater wireless sensor networks (UWSNs) face critical challenges in energy imbalance, connectivity, and data collection due to harsh environments. To address these issues, this paper focuses on the problem is how to achieve energy-balanced data collection in IoT-enabled UWSNs with a mobility-aware mobile edge computing (MEC), named MECEBDC. Unlike existing approaches, the proposed scheme jointly optimizes energy-aware clustering, cluster head selection, and AUV-assisted data collection. Furthermore, we design a novel metaheuristic-based AUV routing algorithm that incorporates realistic underwater mobility dynamics, explicitly considering gravitational pressure and buoyancy forces acting on the AUV. By leveraging the computing, storage, and mobility capabilities of MEC-enabled AUVs, the proposed approach enables efficient trajectory planning and adaptive data gathering in a stable 3D underwater environment. Extensive simulations and theoretical analysis demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces node energy consumption, improves data collection efficiency, and prolongs network lifetime compared with existing schemes, making it well suited for long-term underwater IoT applications.
comment: Presented at the International Conference on Computing and Communication Networks (ICCCNet-2026)

title: Essential Unitarity for Higher-Order Quantum Computation (Extended Abstract)
summary: We develop a boundary-centric semantic framework for higher-order quantum computation, building on the Kelly-Laplaza description of compact closure and Abramsky's execution account. In the semantic carrier Perm(C), morphisms are complex-linear combinations of polarized boundary linkings, composed by execution. Finite-family addresses provide coherent control over finite-level quantum registers (qudits) while retaining the multiplicative boundary structure. We identify essential unitarity, a boundary condition extending ordinary unitarity to higher-order interfaces. On positive qudit registers it coincides with ordinary matrix unitarity; at higher order it expresses preservation of information across the full polarized boundary. We define a unit-free coherent quantum core generated bymultiplicative wiring, unitary gates on positive qudit registers, and contextual coherent control, and prove that every one of its morphisms is essentially unitary. The framework realizes an applied coherent quantum switch and the unitary stages of equal-ratio one-slot supermap dilations with explicit memory. Complete proofs appear in the full version of this paper.

title: How to prove equations using diagrams: A categorical and operational semantics for e-graphs
summary: E-graphs are a powerful algorithmic technique for automated equational reasoning but have resisted a conceptual understanding independent of issues of presentation and implementation. We propose an operational semantics for e-graphs based on the fundamental category-theoretic concepts of diagrams, limits, and initial functors. We illustrate the formalism through numerous example calculations and establish its soundness and completeness. Technical prerequisites are kept to a minimum in the main text; less standard elements of the mathematical theory are developed in two appendices.

title: Neural networks and games
summary: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

title: Sundance: A Simple SMT Solver for Program Verification
summary: We present Sundance, an SMT solver for program verification written in about 13,600 lines of Rust. Sundance combines the Cadical SAT solver with congruence closure, linear arithmetic, algebraic datatypes, and pattern-based quantifier instantiation. Sundance produces eDRAT proofs for every unsat answer. On 21,531 queries from Verus, Dafny, and F*, Sundance is comparable to existing solvers, with 26--38 times fewer lines of code than Z3 and cvc5. We further show that its components can be swapped for Z3's arithmetic solver, MiniSat, and the Semper e-graph. We have open sourced Sundance.

title: The CNF Encoding Complexity of Boolean Functions
summary: We study the minimum number of clauses required to encode a boolean function into a CNF formula with auxiliary variables. Our main result is that if a boolean function can be evaluated in nondeterministic time $t$ (in the RAM model) with $m$ bits of advice such that at most $b$ bits of advice are accessed for each input, then it admits a CNF encoding with $\widetilde{O}(t + \sqrt{mb})$ clauses. This constitutes a nonuniform generalization of Robson's (TCS'91) variant of the Cook--Levin theorem, for which a naïve generalization would yield $\widetilde{O}(t+m)$ clauses; our applications leverage $b = o(m)$ to obtain significantly better bounds. Since preprocessed data structures can be modeled as computation with advice, our result allows us to translate space- and time-efficient data structures to compact CNF encodings. As an application, we derandomize a data structure of Larsen and Williams (SODA'17) to show that every $k$-CNF function on $n$ inputs can be encoded with $n^k/2^{Ω_k(\sqrt{\lg n})}$ clauses. Notably, despite encoding a $k$-CNF function, the encoding itself necessarily contains clauses of unbounded width, since an information-theoretic argument shows that the minimum number of bounded-width clauses to encode such functions is $Ω_k(n^{k}/\lg n)$ in the worst case. In general terms, our results imply that for a wide variety of NP-complete problems, one can reduce to CNF-SAT in a way that results in asymptotically fewer clauses than previously known methods.

title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification
summary: We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.

title: ProofStudio: Five Proof Assistants in the Browser
summary: Recent advances in AI-assisted proof automation are extending the use of proof assistants in software verification and mathematics. However, greater proof automation does not remove users' responsibility to assess whether formal statements capture their intended requirements, making education in formal specification and reasoning essential. To lower the installation and learning barriers associated with mature proof assistants, we present ProofStudio, a browser-based environment integrating Isabelle/HOL, Lean, Rocq, HOL4, and HOL Light with corresponding worked examples, preconfigured proof search, and contextual AI assistance. With ProofStudio, users can explore formal specifications and proofs across five systems without local installation, inspecting native prover feedback and experimenting with automation through a common interface.
comment: The tool is available at: https://proofstudio.org/

title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
summary: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.

title: Solving the Nonlinear Westervelt Equation in Ultrasound Propagation Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Modeling the nonlinear acoustic wave propagation in biological tissues needs accuracy, especially in ultrasound imaging and therapeutic applications. The 1D Westervelt equation, \( p_{xx} - p_{tt} + γ\, p_{ttt} + η\,(p^{2})_{tt}=0, \) could be used to describe a finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in these tissues. This equation accounts for nonlinearity, \(η\), and attenuation, \(γ\). To solve this equation, we observe that traditional solvers may struggle to do so correctly. This is due to the difficulties arising from the nonlinear nature of the equation. We solve the equation by defining three synthetic cases - linear (\(η=0.001\), \(γ=10^{-6}\)), shock-dominated (\(η=0.02\), \(γ=10^{-6}\)), and dissipation-dominated (\(η=0.01\), \(γ=5\times10^{-4}\)) - and using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to showcase the solution. A sinusoidal activation function is used to capture the oscillatory behavior of the problem. The results of our study, with PDE residual converging to at least \(10^{-6}\), boundary condition loss to \(10^{-5}\), and the PINN loss converging to \(10^{-5}\) for each case at \(30,000\) epochs, show that \(γ\) scales the rate of amplitude decay, while \(η\) governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.

title: Global Trace Condition for Injective Transition Graphs
summary: We formulate the global trace condition, GTC, for cyclic proofs as a particular case of the size-change termination condition, or SCT. We express cyclic proofs through a variant of size-change graphs, called transition graphs, whose edges are labelled by (finite) bipartite relations. We show that injective transition graphs suffice to encode cyclic pre-proofs for a variant of Brotherston and Simpson's sequent calculus with inductive definitions. The injectivity of transition graphs corresponds to restricting SCT to fan-in-free graphs. Then we prove that an essentially weaker condition implies SCT in this case, and hence GTC.

title: Refined CMA-ES for CEC 2026 Bound-Constrained Single-Objective Optimization
summary: We present a simplified and parameter-adjusted variant of CMA-ES designed for the CEC 2026 Bound-Constrained Single-Objective Optimization competition. Unlike typical algorithmic developments that increase complexity by adding mechanisms, Refined CMA-ES systematically removes components that do not improve performance, such as the flat-land escape, while retaining standard features that provide measurable benefits. Adjusting key parameters (population size and initial step-size) yields substantial gains, outperforming the baseline CMA-ES and several state-of-the-art competitors. The paper highlights the practical relevance of individual CMA-ES components under the CEC 2026 ranking, which equally weights solution accuracy and convergence speed, demonstrating that simplification combined with improved parameter settings can lead to superior performance.
comment: 4 pages pre-print, accepted to IEEE CEC 2026 as a full paper, published in IEEE CEC 2026 Proceedings

title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
summary: Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories. More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $π(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $ω$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $π(A)$ is nowhere dense. In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $ω$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

title: An ensemble of graph generative models for assisted history matching of the Brugge field case
summary: Assisted history matching remains non-unique because many geological realisations can reproduce equivalent production responses with substantial differences between individual well matches. This ambiguity increases when a field comprises several depositional settings and modelling strategies. The paper applied a graph autoencoder approach to history matching of a benchmark Brugge field that comprises different depositional zones. Each stratigraphic zone is modelled with its dedicated generative model that comprises a joint latent space for optimisation history matching loops. Graph-based generators operate directly on the active cells of the corner-point grid, so its irregular geometry is handled without conversion to a regular lattice. The optimisation search in the 160-dimensional joint latent space is done with the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy. The multi-component objective function includes static well data mismatch, dynamic production mismatch, and a geological realism penalty based on the Decoder induced latent metric. Latent space diagnostics with topological data analysis are applied prior to history matching to test whether one generator is sufficient or whether a multiple generator formulation is required. The results show that the zone-based formulation gives coherent latent spaces, preserves the main porosity and permeability relations that vary from one zone to another, and supports history matching while keeping the solutions within the learned geological manifold. The matched models reproduce field oil and water production within the prior uncertainty range and provide a comparable well-level match to previously published Brugge studies based on Ensemble Kalman Filter, Particle Swarm Optimisation with principal component analysis of parameterisation, and Multiple Kernel Learning with Particle Swarm Optimisation.

title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
summary: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures (6 + 1 Extended Data), 6 Extended Data tables. Demo: https://neovand.github.io/sketchpad/demo ; code (Apache 2.0): https://github.com/NeoVand/sketchpad ; model: https://huggingface.co/mohsenvand/sketchpad-0.8b-preview

title: Aero-VPA: Few-Step Flow-Matching Control over Non-Reconstructive JEPA Latents for Agile Flight on Edge Hardware
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
comment: 38 pages, 3 figures, 22 tables. Simulation study (PX4 SITL + Gazebo Harmonic). Version 2 of a preprint first posted on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23633375). Code: https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA ; trained policy: https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa ; benchmark dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ylee-sling/aero-vpa-benchmark

title: Monodromy Computation Model
summary: A closed path can return to its starting point while analytic continuation reaches another branch. We construct a finite computational calculus in which retained logarithmic branches supply memory, analytic observations select operations, and descent through a covering exposes deeper memory. Three branch coordinates suffice, and every finite observation uses the same cubic power covering. Each program defines a globally real analytic return map whose integer-lattice execution is realized by actual path lifting. Our first theorem simulates every finite-alphabet, finite-control Post--Turing machine, preserving complete configurations, halting, and divergence. Our second theorem identifies the partial numeric functions of the calculus, under fixed primitive-recursive input and output maps, with exactly the partial recursive functions. Deleting descent leaves a Forward language with a syntax-derived finite observation quotient and a primitive-recursive halting predicate. This yields a strict separation within the calculus and identifies access to deeper memory as its decisive additional operation. The constructions and semantic correspondences are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

title: Reasoning about Shared-Qubit Concurrency in Quantum Computing
summary: In this paper, we develop a semantic model for the parallel execution of quantum circuits, providing a formal foundation for studying shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing. As in classical shared-memory concurrency, parallel quantum circuits may interfere with one another through operations on shared qubits. However, quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations introduce additional challenges for reasoning about their correctness. To address these challenges, we generalise the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum computing at the level of quantum circuits. Our approach enables compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits by separating the verification of individual components from the analysis of interference between them. We formulate proof rules for establishing the correctness of parallel quantum circuits and prove their soundness with respect to the proposed semantic model.

title: Attack-Aware Intrusion Risk Monitoring for Aerial Surveillance via Probabilistic Signal Temporal Logic
summary: This paper considers online intrusion-risk assessment and graded warning for unmanned aerial vehicles under bounded measurement attacks. To address this problem, we develop a monitoring framework that combines trusted state estimation, attack-aware risk assessment, and probabilistic signal temporal logic (PrSTL). Trusted observations support recursive state estimation, while potentially attacked observations inform integrity testing and intrusion-risk assessment. The key contribution is a confidence-set construction that combines normalized innovation statistics with physical attack bounds to characterize admissible measurement biases. The resulting family of bias-corrected Gaussian posteriors yields an upper bound on the probability of occupying a no-fly zone or its surrounding safety margin. Confidence guarantees and finite-cover numerical certificates quantify the reliability of this risk envelope, which is evaluated with or without an integrity alarm. The PrSTL monitor analyzes the resulting risk sequence to distinguish ordered, persistent, and repeated risk and produces graded warnings with explicit robustness margins and supporting windows. We validate the monitor in flight experiments with a Crazyflie quadrotor tracked by a Vicon motion capture system. Controlled comparisons quantify the contributions of individual monitoring components. Prescribed risk profiles verify the temporal semantics and illustrate how distinct risk patterns produce different warning levels.

title: Polynomial VASS MDPs
summary: Markov decision process over vector addition system with states (VASS MDP) is a finite state model combining non-deterministic and probabilistic behavior, augmented with non-negative integer counters that can be incremented or decremented during each state transition. VASS MDPs can serve as abstractions of probabilistic programs, offering many decidable properties. In this paper, we develop techniques for analyzing the polynomiality of asymptotic estimates for VASS MDPs. That is, for every initial configuration of size \(n\), we consider the number of transitions needed to reach a configuration with some counter negative. We show that for any VASS MDP, either for all \(ε>0 \) and all sufficiently large \(n\) the number of transitions is at least \(2^{n^{\frac{1}{2}-ε}} \) with probability at least \(1-ε\), or for any superpolynomial function \(f \), all \(ε>0 \) and all sufficiently large \(n\) the number of transitions is upper bounded by \(f(n) \) with probability at least \(1-ε\). Furthermore, if the VASS MDP is DAG-like then we can replace \(f(n)\) with \(n^{k+ε} \), where \(k=2\cdot 3^{w\cdot d+|T|} \) and \(w,d\) and \(T \) are the number of MECs, counters and transitions of the VASS MDP, respectively. It is decidable in polynomial time which case holds.

title: Proceedings 23rd International Conference on Quantum Physics and Logic
summary: This volume contains the proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Quantum Physics and Logic (QPL 2026), which was held from August 17 to August 21 2026, in Amsterdam, The Netherlands, organized by the University of Amsterdam. QPL is an annual conference that brings together academic and industry researchers working on topics ranging from basic research in the foundations of physics to applications in quantum computing and communication, both for near-term quantum hardware and future large-scale, fault-tolerant devices. The conference places particular emphasis on the application of formal algebraic, logical, compositional, and categorical structures to quantum theory and related areas. Work applying quantum-inspired techniques and structures to other fields such as (classical) computation, linguistics, artificial intelligence, and causality is also welcome.

title: Evolved Spiking Neural Networks for EEG Seizure Detection: Calcium Dynamics and Delay Mechanics
summary: Neuroevolution can discover compact network designs that are hard to specify by hand. The EONS framework evolves the topology, weights, thresholds and delays of neuromorphic spiking networks without gradients. We tested whether giving integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons an activity-dependent calcium current (Ca-IF neurons) improves evolved networks for EEG seizure detection, with calcium parameters fixed, shared across a network, or evolved for each neuron. On 10 held-out CHB-MIT patients never seen in training, per-neuron calcium raised the record-level Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.592 to 0.726 over 20 independent runs (p = 0.008) and lowered the false-alarm rate from 0.17 to 0.10. Fixed or per-network calcium gave no significant benefit. IF networks with evolved synaptic delays of 1-3 ticks gave a similar gain (p = 0.005), whereas axonal delays did not. On Siena, with unchanged settings, per-neuron calcium gained +0.096 MCC over IF in one patient-disjoint split (p = 0.011) and +0.059 in the other (p = 0.052). These results suggest that calcium and delays may make the evolutionary search more effective, and motivate testing on more data and in neuromorphic hardware.
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, plus three supplementary tables and one supplementary figure

title: Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks
summary: Understanding how neurons respond to visual stimulus is an important question in both deep learning and neuroscience. It has significant implications for enhancing the interpretability of black-box artificial neural networks and for understanding the visual representation in the human brain. We propose a structured visual representations landscape and design an activation-based prior that allows us to effectively regularize the landscape with activations from brain regions or neural network units. Our model Vis-Lens integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model into an image generation framework. It enables the generation of natural, realistic preferred images by directly modifying the activation-regularized latent codes without per-image iterative optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on both artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Our framework improves activation modulation and image realism compared with a recent state-of-the-art method for generating preferred visual representations of these neural targets. Code is available at https://github.com/NeuroAIHub/Vis-Lens.

title: Final coalgebras over R-modules
summary: Final coalgebras and the coinduction principle for coalgebras over $R$-modules, where $R$ is a commutative ring, are essential in determining the denotational behaviour of various types of linear weighted automata. The goal of this paper is to provide lower and upper bounds on the ordinals that are needed to construct final coalgebras over $R$-modules as the limit of a transfinite sequence of functor iterations. We give an example of a binary intersection preserving finitary functor on the category of abelian groups, which is the category of modules over integers, that fails to converge in $ω\cdot 2$ steps, thus settling an open problem of Adámek, Milius, and Moss. Then we relate this to the failure of the Artinian property of the integers and show that all finitary functors on $R$-modules for a Noetherian ring $R$ with Krull dimension $n$, which preserve countable directed intersections and a generalised notion of monomorphism, converge in $ω\cdot (n + 2)$ steps. We also establish how the connection between Aczel-Mendler bisimulation and behavioural equivalence is mediated by the functor $\operatorname{Ext}^1$. These results show that homological algebra tools can play an important role in coalgebra.

title: Propositional Dynamic Logic with Program Costs
summary: We introduce $\mathbb{N}\mathtt{PDL}$, a resource-aware variant of Propositional Dynamic Logic ($\mathtt{PDL}$) capable of accounting for program costs measured by natural numbers (such as time or space in the sense of computability theory). In this framework, programs correspond to transition systems weighted by extended natural numbers, and the syntax of our logic includes formulas expressing which properties are reachable by program executions within specific cost constraints. First, we explain how the standard program constructs of non-deterministic choice, sequential composition, iteration, and tests are interpreted in this weighted setting and establish the validity of their corresponding reduction axioms. Using an appropriate adaptation of the (Fischer-Ladner) filtration technique, we proceed to prove decidability and completeness for $\mathbb{N}\mathtt{PDL}$ as our main results. We furthermore provide upper and lower complexity bounds for this logic using translations between standard $\mathtt{PDL}$ and $\mathbb{N}\mathtt{PDL}$.

title: Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms
summary: Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^dσ(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Code and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/usamihiroyasu/attention-head-fusion

title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
summary: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.
comment: 35 pages (10-page main text, references, and appendix), 7 figures, 20 tables. Benchmark and harness: https://github.com/specula-org/TLAPS-Bench

title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
summary: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains. The agent integrates the reasoning capabilities of large language models with the formal verification capabilities of the Rocq proof assistant. It incorporates task classification, tool-assisted execution, verification feedback, and state-based task management to support the generation, refinement, and verification of formal proofs. Unlike an approach focused on a single mathematical theory, the agent is examined through case studies involving Morse--Kelley axiomatic set theory (MK), real numbers, propositional logic, and equivalences of the axiom of choice. These cases investigate its applicability across mathematical foundations and distinguish source-level completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of a unified operational framework for heterogeneous foundation-level tasks and clarify the gap between such a framework and a fully integrated mathematical foundation.

title: Iterated Narrow Networks: Turing Completeness at Width 4 on Convex Input Spaces and the Complexity of Verification
summary: We study the iterates of a fixed ReLU network $N$ of width 4, that is, the discrete-time system $x_{k+1} = N(x_k)$ on $[0,1]^4$. Equivalently, $x_k$ is the output of a weight-tied network made of $k$ copies of $N$, or of a recurrent network with no external input, started at $x_0$. We prove that every deterministic Turing machine $M$ admits such a network $N_M$. The network can be constructed in polynomial time from $M$. Each iteration has depth $\mathrm{poly}(|M|)$. The iterates of $N_M$ simulate $M$ exactly on every encoded tape. The number of iterations is proportional to the running time of $M$. Moreover, the fourth coordinate irreversibly flags every point of the convex cube $[0,1]^4$ whose simulation reads an invalid digit. This flag is the certificate that makes hardness reductions sound on convex input regions, the regime of practical verifiers. Convex regions were previously inaccessible because of a continuity obstruction inherent to ReLU networks. The correspondence has three consequences. First, reachability for iterated width-4 ReLU networks spans the full complexity hierarchy along the single axis of the time bound: it is NP-complete for a unary bound, NEXP-complete for a binary bound and RE-complete (undecidable) with no bound. Second, two extra neurons of width suffice to extend the hardness to every common smooth activation: at width 6, the robust verification problem (a promise problem with $δ/2δ$ gap) is NP-complete for $\tanh$, sigmoid, GELU, Swish, ELU, and any polynomial-time-computable continuous non-polynomial activation with a polynomial-time-computable Lipschitz constant. Third, the whole spectrum transfers to discretized Neural ODEs in dimension 5.
comment: 41 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

title: Modern Software Engineering with Verification Agents: A Spec-First Architecture for Autonomous Synthesis, Verification IRs, and Organizational Scale
summary: When autonomous coding agents synthesize implementation code, formal specifications, and mechanical proofs simultaneously, the software engineering hierarchy inverts: the formal specification becomes the primary human-reviewed artifact, while source code and proof scripts become disposable build outputs. This paper presents an end-to-end architecture for agent-authored, formally verified software engineering.
